With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

#3052. Qualys's 2027 Outlook: Achieving Federal Authorization Solidifies Public Sector Moat

This under-the-radar cybersecurity stock boasts a Superscore of 85 from our Hidden Gems Primary database, part of The Motley Fool's Moneyball Database system. Here's why.

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 25, 2026 at 3:53PM EST

When a large enterprise needs to lock down its entire digital footprint, it turns to Qualys (QLYS +2.20%). Picture a security officer managing thousands of servers, cloud containers, and remote endpoints, all of which represent a potential entry point for a breach. Qualys provides the unified platform that identifies those risks and automates the fix, turning a chaotic network into a defensible one. As of November 19, 2026, the stock trades at $192.51, having risen 39% over the past year.

Our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns Qualys an overall Superscore of 85 out of 100, placing it in the Strong category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a company's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39).

An 85 Superscore places the company in the Top ~4% of every company we score, which is ahead of roughly 96 out of every 100 companies we evaluate. This Superscore is one data-driven signal worth investigating, and this article pairs the reasons the score is high with the reasons it is not higher so you can weigh both sides before doing more work.

Qualys is a highly capital-efficient business, earning outsized profits on a small base of hard tangible assets. This efficiency allows the company to turn each point of revenue growth into strong returns, a trait the market often rewards with a premium valuation. While this efficiency is a clear advantage, it does not erase the risks posed by elevated valuation multiples and aggressive competition.

Qualys is well positioned in the cybersecurity space. Organizations and government agencies are shifting to platforms that not only identify security vulnerabilities, but also fixes them. That is one of the company's key strengths, which has grown in importance now that hackers can employ artificial intelligence to quickly attack a system before an organization can respond. As a result, Qualys saw its federal government-related sales outperform expectations in Q3 as agencies consolidated spending onto its platform.

Moreover, while many software companies operate at a loss, Qualys is profitable with an impressive Q3 gross margin of 83%. It sports a fortress balance sheet, exiting the third quarter with total assets of $1.2 billion compared to total liabilities of $536.3 million, and of those liabilities, more than $425 million is deferred revenue, which will transition to sales after services are delivered.

Given the company's many strengths, Qualys is well positioned for years of growth ahead. Yet these factors have contributed to the stock's elevated valuation, with a trailing P/E ratio that's around a high point for the past year. This suggests now is not the best time to buy. #3051. Major MacBook Air ‘overhaul’ could launch next year, per Gurman

Apple has a new MacBook Air with M6 chip coming early next year, but per Mark Gurman on his latest podcast episode, a “big MacBook Air overhaul” could launch as early as 2027 too. Here’s what he said.

Today on the latest episode of Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the well-sourced reporter answered a listener question that involves the future of the MacBook Air.

When asked about the next-generation MacBook Air, here’s what Gurman said:

The next MacBook Air project, J913 and J915, the 13-inch version and the 15-inch version, that is coming in spring 2027 alongside the MacBook Neo 2. And this is going to be another “chip and ship,” so a chip refresh.

We’re now in 2027. MacBook Air is Apple’s most popular computer, and they need to keep it very fresh. And so my anticipation is 2027-2028 is when we’re going to get the big MacBook Air overhaul. And I think OLED will be part of that conversation.

There are several noteworthy takeaways here:

Wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. #3047. Qualcomm vs. Sandisk: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Sandisk's revenue surged over 270%, driven by demand for cloud memory, while Qualcomm is branching into automotive and satellite connectivity. Which chip stock holds up better?

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 25, 2026 at 4:00PM EST

As mobile markets mature and artificial intelligence expands, investors are looking for the next big chip winner. Is Qualcomm (QCOM +2.24%) or Sandisk (SNDK -5.57%) the better choice for your 2027 portfolio?

Qualcomm provides the wireless connectivity and processors that power modern smartphones and connected vehicles. Sandisk specializes in the flash storage and memory solutions required for high-speed data processing in cloud environments. Both companies are essential to the global technology infrastructure, but they offer vastly different financial profiles for investors to consider.

As one of the most prominent semiconductor stocks, Qualcomm designs the high-performance computing and connectivity platforms found in premium handsets and industrial devices. The company relies on a small group of mobile handset customers, including Apple Inc. (AAPL +0.43%) and Samsung, for a significant portion of its revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, particularly as Apple develops its own internal modem technology. To offset this, Qualcomm is expanding into automotive and data center markets while partnering with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) to provide radio platforms for the Starlink Mobile 5G network.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 27, 2026, revenue reached about $43.1 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 2.6% compared to the previous twelve-month period. Despite the slight revenue dip, the company reported a net income of roughly $13.6 billion for that time frame. Net margin for the year was about 32%, showing the company's ability to maintain high profitability even during a period of slowing top-line growth.

The company maintains a solid balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.5x as of its September 2026 balance sheet. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the company maintains a manageable level of borrowing. Its current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, stands at nearly 1.9x. For the fiscal year ended Sept. 27, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $8.7 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 31% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Sandisk operates as a major force in the flash memory industry, serving the massive data center, PC, and mobile device markets. The company provides the hardware necessary for storing and moving the vast amounts of data used by modern artificial intelligence systems. Unlike many chip peers, its sales are highly diverse, with no single customer accounting for more than 10% of revenue in the most recent fiscal year. This broad base of OEM and channel customers helps reduce the impact of any single partnership ending.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached about $29 billion, a significant growth of approximately 272% over the prior year. This rapid expansion was accompanied by a net income of roughly $19.4 billion. The surge in sales and earnings reflects the intense demand for high-capacity memory solutions in the cloud computing sector. The company achieved a net margin of nearly 67% during this period, highlighting the strong demand for its memory technology.

As of July 2026, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, indicating that total liabilities do not exceed shareholder equity and its reliance on debt is minimal. Its current ratio was nearly 2.3x, suggesting a comfortable cushion for meeting its short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended July 3, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $11.5 billion. This robust cash generation allows the company to reinvest heavily in manufacturing facilities and next-generation storage research.

Qualcomm faces significant risks from its revenue concentration among a small number of handset manufacturers. The company expects Apple will transition to its own internally developed modems in the near future, which could impact sales. Furthermore, heavy exposure to the Chinese market makes the company vulnerable to shifting trade policies and national security regulations. Its reliance on a fabless model also means it depends on third-party foundries like Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung for leading-edge production capacity.

Sandisk carries operational risks due to its heavy reliance on joint ventures with Kioxia for memory production. Its manufacturing facilities are geographically concentrated in Japan and Malaysia, leaving the supply chain open to disruption from natural disasters or geopolitical conflict. The memory industry is also notoriously cyclical, with intense competition from Nvidia Corp. (NVDA -3.91%), Western Digital (WDC -0.55%), and Micron Technology (MU -4.53%). The company must also manage the complexities associated with its separation from Western Digital, including potential tax liabilities.

Sandisk appears significantly cheaper based on future earnings estimates, while Qualcomm maintains a slightly higher premium for its diversified connectivity portfolio.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Qualcomm's mobile phone business has been hammered this year, as weak Chinese demand and AI-driven memory shortages have caused handset-derived sales to fall below prior-year levels. Yet the AI boom has an upside for Qualcomm.

At the company's June 2026 investor day, Qualcomm raised its non-handset revenue target to more than $40 billion by 2029, nearly double the prior target of $22 billion. Qualcomm is reportedly partnering with OpenAI to develop smartphone processors with advanced AI capabilities. Analysts see this partnership as a positive for Qualcomm since it would enable advanced agentic AI on smartphone platforms. It would also diminish the business risk of Apple developing its own chips and dropping Qualcomm as a supplier.

Meanwhile, Sandisk shares have undergone remarkable appreciation since its spin-off from Western Digital created the firm as a stand-alone entity in February 2025. Shares went from $49 to more than $2,300 by the middle of 2026. Shares have since undergone an 8-for-1 split and seen a significant retracement of gains.

But the share strength shows just how strong the flash memory market has been for Sandisk. During periods of tight supply and strong market pricing, the company's profit margins can be robust, as they have been during this AI-driven market. Historically, though, high memory prices and low supply are followed by periods of high supply and low prices, which are a risk to Sandisk investors in the long run.

Still, the growth is impressive. Revenue should get near $50 billion 2027, more than double 2026, with Wall Street seeing more than $60 billion in sales in 2028. Net income should triple in 2027, to $34.9 billion, and grow more modestly in 2028.

The choice here is simply: Sandisk is booming and comes at a bargain-basement valuation while Qualcomm's expected improvement is still speculative at the moment. There is risk to Sandisk that one may be buying at the peak of the memory cycle, but it's clearly the better bet for 2027.

#3046. CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Packages Could Be at Risk of Holiday Porch Theft

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

US adults have an average package value of $276.24, yet one-fifth don't use security devices due to costs.

Big holiday sales, like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, are here, but before you click ‘buy,’ make sure you have a plan to protect your package from porch pirates.

CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent thefts. This year, the average package value is $276.24, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

But leaving your packages up for grabs could be a big risk — especially when thieves know holiday gifts are being delivered. On the other hand, some bad actors don’t seem to mind being caught in the act on home security cameras, so are they really enough to deter bad actors? And what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other issues like break-ins,” said CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma said that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and new porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

So while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to plan how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

Lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

“I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” said Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

Among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

You shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

“Delivery boxes have reached a new level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” said Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”

If you don’t want to install a new security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

“Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” said Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”

If you’re looking for a camera that’s off-the-grid, consider the Arlo Go 2. It’s an LTE camera, so it uses a cellular data connection instead of Wi-Fi. It still finds a signal, supports app operation and live video viewing. If you’re looking for a power-over-Ethernet camera that uses a cable connection, the Reolink Duo 3 is a good choice.

Among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

“Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” said Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. #3041. Bambu Lab’s New P3C 3D Printer Brings Advanced Features to the Mainstream

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Now everyday hobbyists have access to some of the latest tech without breaking the bank.

On Tuesday, Bambu Lab took the wraps off its third-generation 3D printer, the P3C. It brings to the mainstream the company’s “tool changer” technology, which was previously reserved for higher-end, flagship models like the $2,500 H3C. Given the P3C costs less than half the bigger model, it might be the perfect gift to get your favorite 3D printing hobbyist for Black Friday.

The big deal here is the introduction of the Swaptek 7-tool changer, which allows you to switch to a different color or material in just 6 seconds, preventing you from having to stop and clean the nozzle every time. The technology produces significantly less waste and allows you to create faster prints.

The tool changer technology also allows you to mix different materials with less of a fuss, so you can use a typical rigid plastic and something like a flexible rubber in a single pass without stopping. It can switch between different nozzle sizes in one job. You can switch between  0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm midprint.

The P3C ships with an integrated sealed AMS 3P filament management system that can store up to seven spools, each of which is on an independent feed path to the printer. You can also connect up to four external AMS units, supporting up to 22 colors.

The P3C is more than just a 3D printer. The Swaptek system supports interchangeable craft tools, letting you cut, draw or emboss on materials.

Bambu Lab also included a few features that make the P3C more approachable to newcomers. The P3C provides full-auto calibration, automatically aligning nozzle offsets and multi-tool heads so you don’t have to do it yourself. There’s also a built-in AI monitoring system that can detect issues like nozzle clogs and purge-bin jams early on. A new health management system will no longer spit out vague or obscure errors when something goes wrong. Instead, the new system will explain the issue in plain language and provide step-by-step troubleshooting right on the screen.

CNET’s 3D printing expert, James Bricknell, hasn’t been able to test Bambu Labs’ latest model yet but is excited about it. “While the P3C didn’t arrive in time for a hands-on, it’s built with the same design language and hardware support as the recently released H3C. If it is anywhere near as good, and I think that’s likely, it’ll be at the top of any serious 3D printing enthusiast’s wish list.”

The P3C 3D printer AMS combo is available now worldwide for $1,149. The combo includes the printer, AMS 3P as well as 5 0.4mm standard PrintTools. Two slots are left open for you to customize. This combo option comes with virtually everything you need to get started printing your works of art and more.

#3039. The Best Dividend Stocks to Buy With $5,000 in November

Here's a reliable high-yield stock, a dividend growth stock, and a turnaround story for you to consider.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 25, 2026 at 4:01PM EST

November is drawing to a close, but you still have some time to put money to work in dividend stocks. Say, $5,000, which could give you a toehold in a reliable high-yield stock like Federal Realty (FRT +1.51%), a dividend growth stock like Visa (V +1.83%), or a turnaround story like Pfizer (PFE +0.00%). Here's a look at each one and why, depending on how you prefer to invest, it could be a good place for your cash before the month is over.

Federal Realty is a bit unique in its strip-mall property niche, owning only around 100 assets. It is focused on being a sharpshooter, and its aim is very good. The proof of that is that it is the only Dividend King real estate investment trust (REIT). You don't string together 50+ annual dividend increases by accident; it requires a strong business model that is executed well in both good times and bad.

Federal Realty's approach is actually pretty simple. It buys properties surrounded by lots of wealthy customers. Then it redevelops the assets to ensure they are attractive to both consumers and tenants, including carefully curating the tenant list. When a property reaches full value, the REIT sells it and starts again with a new asset. That approach isn't particularly shocking, but it is hard to execute well. Federal Realty's dividend track record shows it consistently executes well.

You can find higher-yielding REITs pretty easily, but there's only one REIT that can claim to be a Dividend King. For conservative dividend investors, Federal Realty's well-above-market 4.2% yield should help you sleep well at night, even when the market gets turbulent. A $5,000 investment will let you buy 45 shares.

Visa's tiny 0.75% yield probably won't interest you if you are looking for high-yield stocks. That said, the dividend has grown by more than 370% over the past decade, which is a shockingly large number. If you don't need the income today and can set this stock to dividend reinvest, that kind of dividend growth could easily leave you with a robust income stream when you retire.

Visa is one of the world's largest payment processors. It has long benefited from the ongoing shift from paper currency to cards. It only collects a small percentage of each transaction it processes, but when a company handles 74.2 billion transactions in a single quarter (up 10% year over year), the numbers start to add up. And since the world is increasingly moving toward digital transactions, where paper money isn't an option, Visa is likely to have years of growth ahead. The stock isn't cheap, but given the growth opportunity here, it is probably still worth a look for long-term investors. A $5k investment will let you buy 12 shares.

Pfizer, an iconic drug maker, has a huge 6.2% yield. The average yield on pharma stocks is just 1.3%. The core problem Pfizer is facing is major patent expirations in the next few years, with Eliquis losing protection in 2028 and Vyndamax in 2031. It is a very real problem, but Pfizer is actively working on its pipeline to offset the revenue hit. Only, drug development doesn't work on a schedule, even though patent expirations do.

Investors clearly fear the worst, which could include a dividend cut. However, Pfizer's cash flow still covers its dividend, and it has over $14 billion of cash on its balance sheet. Moreover, the company continues to stand behind not only supporting the dividend at its current level, but growing it over time. Given the company's long history of success in the pharma sector, turnaround investors should give it a look. And even if there were a 50% dividend cut, which is probably a realistic worst-case scenario, the yield would still be over 3%. Five thousand dollars will buy you 178 shares.

No two investors are alike, which is why Wall Street is such an exciting place. When it comes to dividends, you can find boring and reliable dividend stocks like Federal Realty. You can find dividend growth stocks, such as Visa. And you can find turnaround stocks like Pfizer that come with ultra-high yields. Each one is worth a deep dive today.

#3035. A Human and an AI Model (Apparently) Solved the Riemann Hypothesis: What it Means for Future of Math

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The AI-assisted proof is 250,000 pages long, and mathematicians are trying to understand what it says.

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of math’s oldest and most famous unsolved problems. It was originally put forward as a problem in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, and professional and amateur mathematicians alike have made thousands of attempts to solve it. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge has apparently solved the problem with the help of AI, showing that in the battle of humans versus AI, the real winner might be both of them working together.

Alpöge made the announcement on Friday in a four-page document (PDF) on his personal web page.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge said in the announcement. “In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.”

The actual hypothesis itself isn’t the biggest deal since all it does is make it easier to see the distribution of prime numbers. However, math didn’t come to a screeching halt just because the hypothesis hadn’t been proven. There are hundreds of other math theorems along with algorithms and cryptographic encryption methods that operate based on the assumption that the Riemann Hypothesis is true.

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Problems for this very reason. If Alpöge really did solve the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude’s help, it would remove a metaphorical logjam that’s been gumming up the works for over a century and a half. Most of those hundreds of math theorems would be proven as true overnight, and all of those algorithms and encryption methods would be validated. That would make solving the Riemann Hypothesis one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in history.

“It is certainly an exciting time,” Paul Milewski, head of the department of mathematics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET. “The Riemann Hypothesis (or any big theorem) is often not the ‘goal’ of mathematics. They are set up as grand challenges that require the development of new tools, new results along the way and new understanding. It is the ‘voyage’ and not the destination that matters the most.”

As such, the mathematics community wasted no time testing the proof to see whether it was true. Two groups — Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative — independently verified the proof, with many other researchers running their own tests and coming to the same conclusion.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on the achievement,” the two groups said in a joint statement on Saturday.

This is certainly an exciting discovery, but it’s not without its obstacles. Alpöge’s proof was a staggering 250,000 pages of some of the most complex math ever written by a human or a machine. Alpöge provided 17 million lines of Lean code, a programming language specifically made for writing and checking proofs, and that’s how researchers were able to check the work and show it to be true.

The problem is that the average novel is about 300 pages, and that means that Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is approximately 833 novels’ worth of complex math. For reference, the longest work ever produced is World-2023, which holds the Guinness World Record at 100,100 pages. That book is 19 feet tall, and Alpöge’s proof is two and a half times longer.

Despite the logic being verified as true through Lean code, Alpöge still has a major problem. So far, none of the mathematicians or researchers who have attempted to read it have been able to understand what it says.

“I do not understand, and I suspect no human completely understands,” Jon Keating, professor of mathematical physics at the University of Oxford, said in a Numberphile YouTube video. “When I look at that, I’m completely in awe and in wonderment.”

For the problem to be fully solved, the proof has to be read, analyzed and simplified so that it can be translated into readable mathematics, which Alpöge says in his announcement that he’s in the process of doing. All of this has to be done so that Alpöge can publish it in a peer-reviewed journal in such a way that his peers can actually read it. It is only after the mathematics community scrutinizes and accepts Alpöge’s proof that it is considered fully solved.

Aside from being nigh unreadable to humans, Alpöge has otherwise avoided the kinds of drama that other AI-assisted discoveries have faced in 2026.

OpenAI had to backtrack on its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem, which is another Millennium Problem, after the company couldn’t rule out that the AI models it used had access to data from other researchers. Somewhat ironically, one of those mathematicians whose work OpenAI may have  — knowingly or unknowingly — borrowed from was Levent Alpöge, as he and others were pretty close to solving the problem on their own.

Similarly, Claude was credited with finding a new novel enzyme that humans had never seen before. The problem is that computational biologist Mario Rodríguez Mestre had seen this enzyme before and was using Claude to study it further, so it’s uncertain if Claude actually found it independently or used data from Mestre’s research to find it.

The heavy assistance from AI has been met with mostly positive reactions, with most researchers agreeing that the AI usage is justified provided that the proof is proven to be true through peer review. Since no one was particularly close to solving the Riemann Hypothesis, there haven’t been any accusations of Alpöge or Claude stealing work like those prior examples. By and large, most mathematicians are excited about the discovery.

“Even before this, we have seen the power of AI, and this shows that AI trained on hundreds of years of human mathematics can perform amazing tasks,” said Penn State’s Milewski. “I would add that AI didn’t come up with the Riemann Hypothesis, nor did most of the work to prove it, and AI probably doesn’t ‘know’ why it was invented or why it’s important.”

CNET spoke with a few professors about this, and they all echoed Milewski’s sentiment, stating that AI was trained with centuries of human mathematical achievement, so a win for AI is a win for humans too. Jeffrey Lagarias, a professor of mathematics at the University of Michigan, told CNET that “I don’t think this particular proof would have been found without AI.”

Prasad Tetali, head of the department of mathematical sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, said: “It is easy to overestimate the role of AI, and underappreciate decades of human mathematician work that went into it. The AI here is really standing tall and wide on the shoulders of generations of human giants.”

On the AI side of things, influencers are attempting to use the news to hype up the capabilities of AI. Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang said in a post on X that solving the Riemann Hypothesis was a sign that AI superintelligence was close at hand and that humanity should be terrified of the “alien mind that we don’t understand.”

AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky likened the whole thing to a company making enriched uranium that’ll one day result in the end of the human species.

These warnings are hard to take seriously when one considers that Anthropic tried to make Claude solve the Riemann Hypothesis by itself back in August. Claude came up with some cool ideas but ultimately failed to solve the problem alone. For the time being, AI still needs a great deal of human guidance to make these massive discoveries, so the doom-and-gloom proselytizing comes off as a little premature.

To make things even more interesting, a competing Riemann Hypothesis proof was submitted by Alessandro Masullo just a few hours after Alpöge released his. This competing proof is 940 pages long, which is significantly shorter than Alpöge’s proof, and it was an all-human effort with no AI assistance. The proof is months in the making, with Masullo working with mathematician Brian Conrad to bring it up to spec before it hits peer review. When Alpöge posted his proof, Masullo and others thought it wise to submit theirs as well.

This started a “dueling proofs” storyline over the weekend, but it was short-lived. Shortly after Masullo’s proof was posted, multiple people found the types of flaws and omissions that often disprove Riemann Hypothesis proofs. Those issues are in the process of being corrected, and the proof is officially in mid-revision status.

Masullo kept the original proof posted (PDF) in its unedited form, but acknowledges that the proof was rushed to publication so that it could compete with Alpöge and Claude.

“The PDF below was posted on Nov. 20 on Ravi Vakil’s blog,” Masullo wrote on a Google site. “It was never meant to be shared publicly at this stage, and it has been posted in this draft form in response to current circumstances.”

It’s entirely possible that future revisions of Masullo’s work may solve the problems in the early draft and create a fully human proof of the Riemann Hypothesis without AI, but that isn’t happening anytime soon.

This is a lot of information about finding the Riemann Hypothesis, so it’s probably a good idea to briefly explain what it even is. In the 1730s, famous mathematician Leonhard Euler came up with a zeta function as a way to solve the Basel Problem, another mathematical curiosity about the exact sum of the reciprocals of squares. Euler was successful in this endeavor, and the zeta function became a part of mathematics.

Bernhard Riemann picked up where Euler left off and expanded the zeta function to use complex numbers — real numbers mixed with imaginary numbers — using a process called analytic continuation. Riemann used this expanded function to express how many prime numbers there were under a specific number and how tightly those prime numbers were packed together.

This is easy enough to do in your head with small numbers, like figuring out there are four prime numbers under 10, but when the biggest prime number is 41,024,320 digits long, having a function to do it for you is a lot more helpful.

The mechanics of Riemann’s expanded zeta function are quite complicated, and the math-focused YouTube channel Numberphile has an excellent explainer from a professional mathematician (with pictures) if you want to learn more.

The hypothesis concerns the solutions the function yields. Riemann’s version of the zeta function showed that if you plugged in an even negative number, like -2, -4 or -672, the function would always spit out a zero. These are referred to as trivial zeroes, and Riemann proved that this was always true in his original paper.

The Riemann Hypothesis is the conjecture that all the other numbers that would also make a zero — referred to as non-trivial zeroes — follow a very specific formula, which is “½ + it”, where “i” is an imaginary number and “t” is any real number, positive or negative. In short, Riemann believed that there was no other way to generate a zero with his zeta function other than even negative numbers (trivial zeroes) and numbers that followed the “½+it” formula (non-trivial zeroes). Riemann provided some examples of the hypothesis being right but never wrote a full proof of it.

It’s worth noting that not every number that follows the “½+it” formula produces a zero, but that all the numbers that produce a zero will use that formula. It’s kind of the same as saying that all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares.

In the 167 years since the hypothesis was first published, mathematicians have found 12 trillion non-trivial zeroes, and every single one of them fits the above rules. Trillions of other numbers that don’t follow those rules have been tested to find a counterexample, since even one counterexample disproves the hypothesis immediately. Those efforts have produced no counterexamples at all.

This isn’t conclusive proof, but it’s such an overwhelming amount of evidence that mathematicians began assuming that the hypothesis was true, even if no one could prove it. Alpöge’s AI-assisted proof is the first to show in any context that the hypothesis is always true, which, according to Tetali, has implications in prime number understanding, number theory and other branches of mathematics.

“The big job on the math side is to find a human-understandable proof,” Lagarias said. “I would say this is certainly going to happen; there will be such understanding. Already there are several AI digests of the proof breaking it into its component pieces. I have seen one [that’s] 11 pages, 164 pages, 273 pages. There are great ideas to extract from them.”

Here's how to choose between these top-rated sleep trackers in the Black Friday sales

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Type: Smart bandSubscription: Google Health Premium (optional, $9.99/mo)

24/7 tracking gives you a more holistic picture into how your sleep habits affect your energy levels throughout the day. Google's Health app provides a more in-depth look at your sleep compared to the Hatch Sleep Clock, but it doesn't compete with analysis dished out by the Withings.

Type: Contactless matSubscription: Withings+ (optional, $9.95/mo)

If you want lab-grade sleep tracking to troubleshoot what might be waking you up through the night, or stopping you from falling asleep, the Withings is your best option. The sleep tracking and analysis is excellent, with the snore tracking feature especially good for spotting potential sleep apnea.

Type: Smart sunrise alarm clockSubscription: Hatch+ (optional, $5.99/mo)

A great beginner's sleep tracker that focuses on the basics only: time spent asleep, and clear analysis of each sleep cycle. Even better, the Hatch Sleep Clock is a fantastic sunrise alarm clock and white noise machine in one, helping you to fall asleep fast at night and wake up energized each morning.

The past few nights I've gone to bed loaded with sleep tech. I've had the Fitbit Air on my wrist, the Withings Sleep Analyzer tucked beneath my mattress, and the Hatch Sleep Clock on my nightstand. Three of the best sleep trackers we've tested have been dutifully recording every minute of my sleep.

Between them, the Fitbit, Withings and Hatch offer sleep tracking for every person. Whether you're a health aficionado looking to improve your wellbeing or a sleep tracking newbie ready to learn but wary of data overload.

I know exactly what you're getting from each of these top rated sleep trackers and in this guide, I'll help you decide which is right for you. I also know the deals to look out for in the Black Friday sleep and mattress sales. Here's how to track, save and sleep better...

With prices starting at $99.99 from Amazon, the Fitbit Air is well-priced and the cheapest of the bunch. The Withings Sleep Analyzer is nearly double the price at $199.99 on Amazon but it's also a fairly unique piece of tech — you'll struggle to find something similar for less.

At $249.99 on Amazon, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the most expensive of the three. That's $80 more than a Hatch sunrise alarm without the tracking.

All options come with sleep tracking data as standard, but subscription upgrades are available. Fitbit and Withings subscriptions deliver AI-powered insights and advice ($9.99/mo and $9.95/mo respectively). Hatch+ gains you access to the Hatch audio library, for $5.99/mo.

With the Black Friday sales underway I'm keeping an eye out for deals on all three sleep trackers. Based on recent sales, I have high hopes for discounts from Withings and Hatch, but I'm less convinced we'll see a deal from Fitbit.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

At just $99.99 from Amazon, the Fitbit Air is an affordable screenfree fitness tracker. In comparison, the Garmin CIRQA and Whoop smart bands start at $199 on Amazon. There's a small chance of a discount this Black Friday but the bulkier Fitbit Inspire is more likely to see a drop. Google Health Premium is available from $9.99, if you want help interpreting your data.

We're hoping to spot money off the Withings Sleep mat over Black Friday but be prepared for flash sales. If you see the price drop to around $159, it's time to shop. A Withings+ subscription adds analysis from $9.95 a month but basic tracking data is included for free.

The Hatch Sleep Clock is $249.99 at full price — $80 more than the Hatch Restore 3 sunrise alarm clock without the tracking. We spotted a discount on the Sleep Clock during the Prime Day sales in October so we're keeping our fingers crossed for another deal.

Design highly influences the user case for all three sleep trackers, so think carefully about which works best for your needs.

The Fitbit Air is a screenless smart band. It sits on your wrist and features a slim pebble tracker integrated into a band. It's not the most fashion-forward smartwatch but it's subtle. The Fitbit Air works best when worn 24/7.

Both the Withings Sleep Analyzer and Hatch Sleep Clock are contactless trackers. The Sleep Analyzer is a mat fitted with sensors that slips under your mattress and connects to a power outlet. It's a tracker you can set and forget.

Hatch's Sleep Clock sits on your nightstand and the attractive casing will suit most decors. Like the Withings, it stays plugged in and you can mostly leave it be. Unless you bump it out of position every morning as you turn off the alarm (not that I'm speaking from experience).

Fitbit, Withings and Hatch sleep trackers all break your rest down into stages (light, deep sleep, and REM sleep) and they all track your latency and wake up time. In other words, they all provide the basics.

But they go about it in slightly different ways. All of them measure big movements, like tossing and turning, while the Hatch captures the micro movements of your breathing and the Fitbit tracks heart rate. The Withings gathers both heart rate and breath rate.

Looking at one night's sleep, you can see a lot of overlap in my data. All three trackers captured me falling asleep and quickly entering deeper sleep, before cycling through the sleep stages for the rest of the night. They also all spot a noticeable interruption in the early hours.

Based on my recollections, Withings overestimates my sleep time. I can pinpoint the problem. That sudden burst of REM sleep around 7.30 a.m.? That's me scrolling through my phone. It's a problem I've experienced before with Withings, while Fitbit and Hatch accurately assess I was awake.

However, Fitbit has its own problem. Both Withings and Hatch captured that once I'd gotten into bed, I fidgeted, scrolled and listened to music before settling down to sleep. While I wouldn't consider that time period actively trying to sleep, 'revenge bedtime procrastination' is an important part of my sleep hygiene that Fitbit overlooks.

Where Hatch lags behind is data collection. It shows you how much time you spent in bed and when each stage occurred but there's no further detail. There's not even a sleep score, although Hatch does offer positive feedback.

The Withings comes out on top when it comes to sheer data. You get hours in bed, movement, respiratory rate, heart rate and HRV. It also has snore detection — a helpful stage in identifying sleep apnea.

Fitbit delivers your sleeping heart rate, but it's a bit of a buried metric. What Fitbit excels at is putting your sleep into context. It compares your nightly averages to help you identify sleep trends.

Overall, all three trackers deliver data that largely collates with my recollection of the night. Withings wins for in-depth data but can struggle to differentiate a 'lazy morning' from 'oversleeping'. Fitbit offers accuracy and easy-to-read data but can overlook the bigger sleep hygiene picture. And Hatch keeps things accessible and simple — perhaps too simple, for some.

It's not just about the tracking. Having used all three sleep trackers for several months, here's everything you need to know:

The Fitbit Air is the least comfortable of the three to sleep in. (Although for a smart band, it's pretty comfy.)

I've woken up to smartwatch skin rash more than once. And despite its thin build, I advise side sleepers to wear it on the arm they don't lie on.

But if comfort is top priority, the contactless Withings and Hatch trackers win hands-down. Siting on your nightstand, the Hatch Sleep Clock doesn't impact comfort at all. And the Withings Sleep Mat is a princess and the pea scenario — if you can feel it under the bed, I suggest investing in a thicker mattress.

From a purely aesthetic level, the Hatch Sleep App is my winner. The pastel colors and refined design echo Hatch's build. I'm a big fan of the 'rainbow' shaped sleep tracking, which makes even 3 a.m. wakeups look pleasant.

However, one of the reasons the Hatch app is so appealing is the lack of data. With less to show than Fitbit and Withings, the display is clearer.

Fitbit connects to the Google Health App. A dedicated 'sleep' tab displays all the info you need, including a break down of your night. It's ideal for digging down into sleep stages with easy to read graphics displays are easy to read.

In the Withings app, sleep is displayed in a similar way. However, Withings adds more physiological data, including heat rate and breathing. This snapshot is better at providing deep insight into your overall nighttime health.

Again, the Withings and Hatch have a strong advantage. Both contactless devices are plugged in 24/7. There's no need to charge, so you won't miss out on data due to a dead battery.

The Fitbit Air can last as long as 7 days on a single charge, but let the battery run too low and you'll get some blanks in your data. However, the advantage here is that the Fitbit Air tracks on the go. A must for the frequent traveler.

The Withings Sleep Analyzer only tracks your sleep, although Withings users can connect to other smart home devices. (Mine links to my Withings ScanWatch 2, so my sleep and activity are collated in one app.)

As one of the best fitness trackers we've tested, the Fitbit Air monitors activity throughout the day. It's the best option for providing an all-round view of your health. It also has a built-in smart alarm which vibrates when it detects light sleep (within a set window). I was skeptical wrist vibrations would be enough to wake me but I can attest it's a gentle and effective start to the day.

And the Sleep Clock by Hatch doubles up as a sunrise alarm clock (plus a white noise machine). You set an alarm and the Hatch slowly floods the room with light in the preceding period. This provides the serotonin and cortisol boost of sunshine, even on a dark morning.

The Fitbit Air is the only option that tracks 24/7. If you want to know how your sleep interacts with your fitness and recovery, this is the way to go. Google's Health app also does an excellent job at displaying how you spent every second of your night and comparing it to your overall patterns.

But if you want a sleep tracker you can forget about, the Withings Sleep Mat is ideal. Snore tracking is also a good way to identify sleep disruptions and spot potential sleep apnea. The Sleep Analyzer collects and displays more data than the Fitbit or Hatch too, including HRV and breathing interruptions.

The Hatch Sleep Clock excels as a sunrise alarm clock and white noise machine, while sleep tracking is an enticing add-on for those prioritizing self care and sleep health. It also keeps things simple: time in bed and sleep stages. You learn about your rest without getting overwhelmed, making it ideal for beginners.

#3032. Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3

According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”

The new Google Wallet app brings Gemini agentic shopping to US-based iOS users - sorry, no tap-to-pay.

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone users in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits

The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

There used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

One of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google announced AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.

#3030. An Unsecured Database Exposed About 2 Billion Login Records

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

The files included passwords and data that can keep you signed in. The number of people affected is unknown.

A database containing about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible online without a password, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler said in a report published Tuesday by ExpressVPN. The collection included usernames and passwords tied to email, social media, shopping and financial services. Among the files was an ad offering access to email accounts sorted by geography.

The 2 billion figure is an estimate and not representative of the number of people affected, since some accounts may appear more than once and one person can have dozens of logins saved on a single device. Fowler reported the database to its hosting provider, which restricted public access several days later. It’s unclear how long the files had been exposed or who else may have accessed them.

Fowler’s estimate of about 2 billion login records applies to the database he found. Wired put the total at more than 3.5 billion by including a separate database that security firm UpGuard disclosed last week. That database held about 1.64 billion records, including Chinese national ID numbers, phone numbers and school enrollment records.

Some of the files Fowler reviewed appeared to be from infostealers — malicious software that collects saved passwords and other data from infected devices. Once that information is collected, brokers can buy it in bulk, sort it by country or account type and resell it in smaller batches. A buyer interested in email accounts in a particular country can pay for that slice of the data. The people selling it can make money from the same records more than once.

Fowler saw signs that the files came from multiple sources, but couldn’t determine who assembled the collection or whether it was used for sales, research or another purpose.

I saw a version of that business in my reporting on the dark web for CNET. On Genesis Market, buyers could shop for stolen accounts by location and category, including banking, email and social media. By the time authorities disrupted the marketplace in 2023, it had offered access to data from more than 1.5 million compromised computers, according to the Justice Department.

You can look up your email address in Have I Been Pwned to see whether it appears in a known data exposure. A clean result only tells you what’s in the service’s index.

If you see an unfamiliar login or suspect your device is infected, use a different, trusted device to change the affected password and sign out of other sessions. Start with your email if several accounts may be affected, since that’s where password reset links often go. Replace reused passwords with unique ones, use a password manager to keep track of them and turn on two-factor authentication where it’s available.

Identity theft protection services monitor for signs that your personal information has been exposed or misused. In a leak like this one, an alert about an exposed password can tell you which account to secure, especially if you’ve reused that password elsewhere. Aura is one of the services we tested for CNET’s guide to the best identity theft protection services.

#3029. The Dividend ETF I'd Choose to to Generate $500 a Month in Passive Income

It checks off a few boxes that make it a great fit for long-term investors.

By Stefon Walters – Nov 25, 2026 at 4:15PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF ›

An extra $500 monthly has a nice ring to it. It could cover a couple of bills, a few grocery store runs, or simply sit in your savings for a rainy day. Either way, bringing in $500 monthly with no extra work is hard to beat.

There are plenty of dividend stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to choose from, but I'm a fan of the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD +1.15%) because it's a trifecta: diversified, high-yield, and cheap. It's a dividend ETF you can trust and treat as a set-it-and-forget-it investment.

SCHD only holds 102 stocks, but they're well-established and vetted for quality. To be included in the fund, a company needs to be in good financial standing, have paid dividends for at least 10 years, and have increased its annual dividend for at least five years. Of course, some of its holdings can hit rough patches (as every company does), but those that check those boxes are usually built to last.

SCHD's holdings include 11 Dividend Kings (companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend increases), including four in its top 10 holdings: Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Abbott Laboratories. Together, these four account for over 17% of the ETF, and Dividend Kings account for over 27% (as of Nov. 23).

SCHD can be a good complement to investing in the S&P 500 because it's not as tech-heavy as the index or many other popular indexes and ETFs. Most of its holdings come from more "boring" sectors like consumer staples (19.97%), healthcare (19.20%), and energy (15.38%).

Dividend yields move in the opposite direction of stock prices, so SCHD's 25% surge this year (as of Nov. 23) has pushed its yield down a bit. At the time of writing, its yield is 3.1%, which is below its average over the past three years, but it's still one of the highest yields you'll find in a major dividend ETF or blue chip dividend stocks.

Since SCHD is an ETF, its quarterly payouts aren't as straightforward as individual stocks. When Coca-Cola, for example, sets an annual dividend of $2.12, you know you'll get four $0.53 payouts. SCHD's holdings pay dividends at different times, so SCHD's payout fluctuates. But based on yields, here is how much you'd need invested to generate $500 monthly ($6,000 annually):

Generating $500 monthly from SCHD won't happen overnight for most investors, but it's an ETF you can comfortably add to over time and trust to compound toward your target. Ideally, you'd reinvest your dividends to buy more SCHD shares and speed up the process. The earlier you start, the better.

You don’t have long left to watch these Netflix movies

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix is always adding new movies to its already-large library, but the flip side is that each month, it also removes a bunch of familiar favorites. So, while you might prioritize the new Netflix additions, it's worth making time to watch some soon-to-depart movies while you still have the chance.

On December 1, 2026, Netflix is set to remove 37 movies from its library. This includes my favorite movie of all time (and its equally five-star sequel), a beloved '80s coming-of-age story, and a very intense thriller that stars the late, great Patrick Stewart. And these are just some of the movies that are leaving.

That's a big number, which is why I've combed through the list and picked out a more manageable selection of five great movies you need to watch before they wave Netflix goodbye. Plus, I've also included the full list of movies being removed from Netflix on December 1, if you want to pick your own.

In the headline, I called “Alien” a “sci-fi masterpiece,” and if anything, that’s underplaying my love of this titan of the genre. It’s my favorite movie of all time, and it started my favorite media franchise. This 1979 horror introduced the world to the Xenomorph, and the terrifying alien creature has been a staple of pop culture since. Directed by Ridley Scott, and with a star-making turn from Sigourney Weaver, it’s more than worthy of its enduring legacy.

The premise is simple: a group of deep-space truckers is awoken from hypersleep when their ship alerts them to a strange transmission on a nearby planet. The source of the signal brings pure terror onboard, as they encounter a lethal predator, perfectly formed to kill. The almost-as-good sequel, “Aliens,” is also leaving Netflix on Dec. 1, so make sure you stream them both quickly. Trust me, they make for the perfect sci-fi double-bill.

Watch "Alien" on Netflix until December 1

The entertainment world mourned the great Patrick Stewart last month, so it feels like a fitting time to recommend “Green Room.” This thriller is noteworthy because Stewart plays against type. He’s not playing a hero or a warm father figure, but instead the veteran actor plays the leader of a neo-Nazi group. And he’s chilling! The movie was also the final film released in Anton Yelchin’s lifetime. The actor tragically passed away in 2016, at just 27.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

In “Green Room,” members of a scrappy punk band are booked to play a dive bar, which they soon discover is actually a clubhouse for a neo-Nazi group. After witnessing a member of the group commit murder, they are trapped in the green room backstage and have to fight their way out. Also starring Imogen Poots and Callum Turner, “Green Room” is fast-paced and very loud, not to mention splattered with fake blood. It’s a hoot, and seriously intense.

Watch "Green Room" on Netflix until December 1

Netflix is removing “The Karate Kid”, its two original sequels released in 1986 and 1989, and the 2010 remake soon. I have a soft spot for the remake (please, flame me in the comments!), but I can’t deny that the 1984 original is the true classic in the bunch. One of the most iconic and beloved coming-of-age movies of all time, this flick is charming, relatable, and very good fun.

Daniel LaRusso (Ralph Macchio) moves from New Jersey to Los Angeles, California, and finds the transition tough. Things only get worse when he’s harassed by the students of the Cobra Kai dojo, led by Johnny Lawrence (William Zabka). But Daniel learns to stand up for himself when his apartment's handyman, Mr. Miyagi (Pat Morita), takes him under his wing and teaches him karate. This gives Daniel confidence and a new perspective.

Watch "The Karate Kid" on Netflix until December 1

Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks are a classic romantic-comedy pairing, having starred in “Joe Versus the Volcano,” “You’ve Got Mail” and “Sleepless in Seattle.” Each flick sees them playing characters who fall in love across the movie’s runtime. It’s 1993’s “Sleepless in Seattle” that’s waving goodbye to Netflix next week, but make sure to give it a watch before then if you want a charming rom-com. Yes, it’s sappy, but I dare you not to get emotional.

Architect Sam Baldwin (Hanks) moves from Chicago to Seattle with his eight-year-old son, Jonah (Ross Malinger), after the death of his wife. Aware his father is struggling to come to terms with the loss, Jonah calls a national radio station to find his dad a new wife. Listening in is Annie Reed (Ryan), a Baltimore reporter, who falls for Sam, despite being engaged. It’s a very 1990s plot for a movie; these days, Jonah would have probably just posted a TikTok.

Watch "Sleepless in Seattle" on Netflix until December 1

Jessica Chastain recently starred in the Netflix Original thriller “Heartland,” which, according to many critics (including TG’s Alix Blackburn), is a bit of a misfire. However, one Chastain-led movie that does hit the mark is “Zero Dark Thirty,” a sprawling political thriller from director Kathryn Bigelow, which was nominated for a clutch of Oscars including Best Picture. Its chunky 157-minute runtime might put some viewers off, but give the film your full attention, and you’ll be richly rewarded with a gripping war movie.

Chastain plays Maya Krauser, a fictional CIA intelligence analyst, with a singular focus. Her mission is to find terrorist leader Osama bin Laden, and her determination borders on and then crosses over into obsession. Set over multiple years, “Zero Dark Thirty” chronicles the decade-long manhunt for the man responsible for the world-altering September 11 attacks.

Watch "Zero Dark Thirty" on Netflix until December 1

On December 1, 2026, Netflix is set to remove 52 movies from its library (per What's on Netflix). The movies removed are subject to change.

#3027. Apple TV just won prestigious award for hit drama series

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for Black Friday) won big at this year’s Emmy Awards thanks to Widow’s Bay, and this week at the International Emmys, the streamer triumphed again as Carême won the top Drama Series prize.

Apple TV had a record-breaking year at the Emmy Awards this fall, with 29 wins overall—beating HBO as the most-awarded network.

Apple TV’s acclaimed and provocative French hit “Carême” won Drama Series, marking the second time Apple has landed the coveted award following a win in 2024 for “Drops of God.” Recently renewed for a second season and currently filming in Paris, “Carême” stars César Award winner Benjamin Voisin and is directed by Martin Bourboulon.

Carême is based on the book “Carême: The First Celebrity Chef” by Ian Kelly. It premiered on Apple TV last spring and was acclaimed by critics, garnering a 95% Rotten Tomatoes score.

The show follows the story of Antonin Carême, who “rose from humble beginnings in Paris to the height of culinary stardom in Napoleon’s Europe.” Per Apple: “While he dreams only of becoming the most famous chef in the world, his talent and ambitions attract the attention of renowned and powerful politicians who use him as a spy for France.”

Season 2 of Carême was announced earlier this fall, and is expected to premiere in 2027.

I loved Carême’s first season and definitely recommend checking it out if you’re up for a French-language series.

#3026. Nvidia Is Also Trying to Fix the Bug Causing Excessive SSD Writing

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Computer Accessories > Components > Graphic cards

Nvidia has issued software updates, but it's unclear if the problem is completely fixed.

Nvidia has had its share of drama lately, with the ousting and sudden un-ousting of CEO Jensen Huang after it was discovered he’d had multiple affairs, including one that involved an alleged member of a Chinese spy network. The fallout from the revelations was so significant that some worried Huang’s fate could be a major disruptor to the health of international markets and the future of the entire AI industry.

Given that, the world’s largest semiconductor company possibly wishes its biggest problem were software-related. But that won’t be much comfort to PC users affected by a software bug in Nvidia’s graphics driver that has caused some to experience excessive writes to their solid-state drives.

The issue began popping up in mid-November as posts on Nvidia’s support forums, as well as on Reddit and sites like HardForum, reported seeing as much as 30GB to 70GB of data per hour written to their SSDs. These types of drives wear down quickly over months of such use.

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and hasn’t made any public statements on the issue, but did acknowledge it in a hotfix and subsequent software update for its Windows 11 GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.40, where it said under Fixed General Bugs, “Excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background.” The driver that appeared to have caused the problems was released on Nov. 12.Some tech experts on social media had been suggesting rolling back to older graphics drivers before the hotfixes were released and warned that letting the problem go unchecked could cause an SSD to eventually fail.

Described by WCCF Tech as “a hotfix for the hotfix,” the new update appears to fix the issue in ways that the previous fix did not.

Nvidia’s software problem closely mirrors an issue AMD had with its own Adrenalin Edition graphics software just weeks ago. As of Nov. 18, AMD was still making tweaks to its graphics software to iron out any lingering problems.

PCGamer offered a way to check if your PC is affected by the excess writing issue.

Open Task Manager, click on the Details tab and right-click on the columns at the top to select “I/O write bytes” as one of your Task Manager columns. By doing that, you can see if the file “NVDisplay.Container.exe” is writing a huge amount of data to your data drive.

If that’s the case, you should update immediately to Nvidia’s latest drivers for the fix. In fact, it might be a good idea to update whether you’re experiencing high write rates or not, just to be safe.
