#3025. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”

#3024. Is Berkshire Hathaway Stock a Buy if the Fed Keeps Raising Rates?

Berkshire Hathaway has both opportunities and challenges in a high-rate environment.

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 25, 2026 at 4:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Interest rates are on the rise. At least that's the expectation for most experts. "The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves," warns economist Anthony Smith.

Rising rates have various impacts on different stocks. Some companies experience a net benefit. Others are clear losers in a rising rate environment. Most, however, have a mix of benefits and drawbacks.

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%) is one of the market's most fascinating cases. The conglomerate owns dozens of businesses across dozens of sectors. Breaking down exactly how the company will fare in a rising rate environment can be difficult.

But there are three major moving pieces to pay attention to right now. Let’s look at each.

Warren Buffett is no longer the CEO of Berkshire. But in his final years, he amassed a sizable cash position for the company. In 2016, Berkshire had less than $100 billion in cash. When Buffett stepped aside last year, he left the firm with a record cash position of more than $350 billion.

Investors were curious to see what would happen to all this capital once Greg Abel took over as CEO. So far, Abel has accumulated even more cash. Berkshire's cash pile reached $377.4 billion last quarter.

For every 0.25% increase in interest rates, Berkshire will earn nearly $1 billion in additional interest income annually. So while elevated cash may or may not be in the best interests of shareholders long term, higher interest rates should directly result in higher interest income.

Berkshire is heavily diversified. But at its core sits a portfolio of insurance operations that generate investable cash. When rates rise, insurance operators typically generate more cash to invest -- a positive result for Berkshire shareholders.

"Modestly rising interest rates are generally positive for the insurance industry," concludes the U.S. Office of Financial Research. "When rates rise at a reasonable pace, portfolio yields also rise. With these new, higher-yielding corporate and other bond purchases, insurers' investment earnings also increase."

Again, Berkshire is so diversified that the benefits its insurance operations experience from higher interest rates may be offset elsewhere. But investors can generally expect better interest income from the company's insurance businesses -- similar to what Berkshire will experience for its cash position.

Most of Berkshire's value isn't tied to insurance profits or interest on its cash position. Warren Buffett's primary wealth-creation strategy has been his investing acumen.

Over more than 60 years, Buffett generated compound annual returns of nearly 20%. That's almost double what the S&P 500 index averaged over the same period. That resulted in a cumulative gain of more than 6,000,000% compared to only around 46,000% for the market overall.

Buffett's investing relies on two key levers: public investments and private transactions.

Research on how interest rates impact public stock prices and private market valuations is mixed. Companies that now need to borrow at higher interest rates -- including unprofitable businesses, capital-intensive enterprises, and companies with distant cash flows -- may see their valuations suffer. Certain financial, energy, and tech businesses, meanwhile, may benefit for a variety of reasons.

In short, it's hard to predict how markets in general will respond to changing interest rates. Berkshire may see its stock portfolio perform well or poorly. Similarly, while the company may find more attractive deals -- either on public or private markets -- it may have to shoulder higher debt costs to finance the purchase if cash isn't used. If cash is used, Berkshire forgoes the potential for greater interest income.

All of this means that for a diversified investment conglomerate like Berkshire, investors shouldn't put too much emphasis on the current rate environment. Undoubtedly, Berkshire will be impacted by changing rates. But it has the potential to benefit or suffer in nearly any rate environment. The key to Berkshire's success will remain its long-term investment performance, not near-term shifts in interest rates.

#3022. This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

No, your phone isn’t listening to you. But what about your Apple Watch? I’ve been testing new Audio Intelligence features that record conversations around me, and despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

Marvell's strong growth can be attributed to robust demand for its data center products, which are being deployed to handle AI workloads. Lumentum has been growing significantly faster than Marvell, reporting an incredible 136.5% year-over-year increase in revenue in the previous quarter to $1.26 billion. Lumentum's non-GAAP operating margin shot up by 23.6 percentage points year over year to 42.3% last quarter, leading to a jump of over 4x in adjusted EPS to $4.57.

Lumentum has been benefiting from the incredible demand for optical networking components in AI data centers, as these components address a key bottleneck by enabling the rapid transport of large data sets within AI chip clusters. Not surprisingly, the demand for these components significantly exceeds supply, which is why Lumentum's margins and earnings have been growing at an astronomical pace.

The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2028, and Marvell estimates it will increase its total addressable market (TAM) by $90 billion. Moreover, the acquisition should give Marvell's bottom line a nice boost, as Lumentum's operating margin was higher than Marvell's reading of 37% in the most recent quarter.

Additionally, Marvell expects a run rate of more than $1 billion in annual synergies once the acquisition closes. So, Marvell seems like a long-term winner, and the incredible earnings growth that it is poised to deliver could make investors significantly richer.

Analysts are expecting Marvell's adjusted earnings per share to increase by 49% in fiscal 2027 to $4.22. The forecast for the next couple of years indicates that Marvell's bottom-line growth will be in the 70%-plus range.

As such, investors looking for a top growth stock to capitalize on the AI boom may consider buying Marvell on the dip ahead of its earnings report next week, as strong results and guidance could send the stock soaring once again.

Things change as we get older, but there's a way to hack your system

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we get older, things change, and while I don't necessarily recommend that someone swap their entire routine just because of a number, there are certain factors to consider, especially as you pass the 40 mark.

This applies to both men and women, but particularly women, whose hormones change with perimenopause and menopause, which impacts lean muscle mass and joint and bone health. But regardless, sarcopenia (the age-related, progressive loss of muscle mass, strength, and physical function) begins to accelerate through the 40s and 50s and still applies to everyone.

For that reason, there are a few tweaks we can make to help the transition, and I'm going to lay them out for you below using my experience as a personal trainer and fitness editor.

I absolutely refuse to change someone's gym program just because of a number. Instead, I listen to the client and their goals, potential health conditions, injuries, or life experiences, and I also program to my clients' abilities and scale accordingly.

In fact, I train my 72-year-old dad like he's 30 years younger and he's stronger and more mobile than ever.

That said, people over 40 may notice slower recovery times and changes to joint mobility, strength, or muscle mass. This is a period of time when I think building and maintaining muscle becomes extremely important for function, balance and performance.

For some, it may be possible to remain doing high-impact cardio or HIIT routines, but for many, I see a gradual shift toward low-impact routines such as Pilates or yoga and strength training, which may involve lifting weights at home or in the gym.

Changes to hormones and lower collagen levels mean muscles may take slightly longer to repair and recover from workouts, which makes overtraining easier to accidentally fall into.

Lower collagen levels can also impact your joints, which play a vital role in mobility; tendons and ligaments will also lose elasticity with age, which means you'll need to really focus on proper warm-ups and cool-downs to maintain range of motion without injury or strain.

Alongside sarcopenia, which I mentioned earlier, bone density decreases into your 40s and 50s as well, impacting balance and strength, which can make the likelihood of injuries or falls higher.

#3018. Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the company responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the company can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

Apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:

“The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed new (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s new restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”

As for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”

Arguments by the Little Tech Association, AAI, Public Knowledge, and the EFF all follow a similar line, with some also addressing how Apple’s restrictions on external payment links could affect consumer choice, pricing, and competition.

With temporary threads, any searches you run in Google’s AI Mode won’t be associated with your account or saved to your chat history.

Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training

New to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

This option is currently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a new thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:

“Temporary threads will not be saved to your Google account and disappear after 24 hours,” Google said on a support page. “They won’t be used to train Google’s generative AI models, unless you submit feedback or it’s necessary for safety purposes. Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”

Google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

#3016. Porch Pirates Don’t Care About Your Doorbell Camera. Follow This Expert Plan Now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Soda was stolen moments after delivery. One expert says it's a common tactic.

Doorbell cameras may seem like a good way to make a porch thief think twice, but the reality doesn’t quite match up. Some porch pirates don’t care about being caught on camera as long as they’re able to steal your package, and it’s unlikely that law enforcement will track down the stolen goods.

That’s the case for my fellow CNET editor, Gael Cooper, who had her Amazon delivery stolen a few weeks ago and spotted the thief on camera. It wasn’t expensive tech or a snazzy holiday gift — it was $36 worth of soda.

“When Amazon emailed me that the order was delivered and it wasn’t there, I was very confused,” Cooper said. “When I pulled up the Ring footage, I saw the delivery happen on video, but then, 10 minutes later, a man in a blue hooded coat who’s intentionally hiding his face shows up and grabs the box.”

Package theft cases like this happen year-round, with CNET findings showing that 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or have stopped an attempted theft. And experts predict more stolen packages during the holidays, when thieves expect more deliveries.

So, don’t give thieves a chance. Now’s the time to make a plan to keep your Black Friday and Cyber Monday packages out of sight. But what tactics actually work if doorbell cameras don’t? Here’s what you should know about porch piracy and how to lessen your chances of package theft.

Cooper’s Amazon order was scheduled to arrive between 3 a.m. and 6 a.m. — when it’s dark, but she knew she would be home. But thieves were already out lurking during those hours. Cooper said the thief followed the driver and stole the package. She saw the thief stealing the package on her Ring security camera system.

Greg Zakowicz, Omnisend’s e-commerce and retail advisor, said Cooper’s package-theft incident is fairly typical, unfortunately — especially during the holiday season.

“Thieves know as well as shoppers that orders increase during this time, and often, the packages are more likely to contain more valuable items,” said Zakowicz. “Shoppers during this time look to take advantage of deep discounts for not only gifts but themselves, making the package a potential goldmine for thieves.”

There are a few steps you can take to lessen the likelihood of porch piracy. Zakowicz recommends using options like in-store pickups, post office boxes, in-garage delivery or deliveries to your workplace.

That advice is especially important for expensive tech you plan to have delivered to your home unless someone will be there to grab the package immediately.

“While it may be less convenient, it’s a small price to pay to not have the hassle of gifts and expensive items going missing at the busiest shopping time of the year,” said Zackowicz.

Also ask your retailers not to ship the item in the manufacturer’s packaging. Some retailers, like Amazon and Target, will clearly display this before shipping because it could be an easy hint for thieves to guess what it is — especially if it’s tech. Even though this won’t stop porch pirates from being curious about what’s in the box, it may make them think about the effort and risk versus the potential reward, Zakowicz said.

If you want another option to have packages delivered to your home, consider scheduling your deliveries for a time you know you’ll be available. For instance, you can set up an Amazon Day to have all of your Amazon packages delivered at once so you can plan accordingly.

CNET found that US adults have mixed feelings about how effectively security cameras deter porch pirates: 11% of US adults believe they don’t deter them, while 9% use security cameras to get proof — not prevent it.

Regardless of your home security measures, don’t assume you’re safe from porch pirates just because you have a doorbell camera, and don’t use it as a means of keeping an eye on your package if you’re busy or not home. Instead, when you see motion detection, that’s a sign to grab it right away.

“The most common misunderstanding is that having security cameras will prevent thieves from stealing packages,” said Zakowicz. “Thieves are thieves because being caught is not their biggest worry. They also know porch piracy is not at the top of most officers’ day-to-day public service worries. Often, by the time the report is made, thieves are long gone.”

Unfortunately, thieves may find other ways to steal packages, since their tactics are constantly changing. If that happens to you, there are a few steps you should take right away.

File a police report of the incident first. Be prepared to share information, including a description of the thief, and the make and model of the vehicle, with the police and your community so they can be vigilant of the thief.

But don’t get your hopes up that the thief will be caught. Zakowicz said it’s rare that porch theft cases get solved.

“Police aren’t necessarily dedicating resources to solving porch pirates who stole a new stuffed animal or board game. However, it’s important for them to understand areas seeing an uptick in thefts, as they can be more alert to suspicious activity,” said Zakowicz. And the retailer may request it.

After filing, Zakowicz says to report the theft to the carrier and retailer. Carriers may use the data to assess future likelihood of package theft incidents and it could help instruct delivery drivers to carefully hide packages. Retailers may also be able to assist with a replacement.

Cooper filed a police report with her local police department, which allowed her to upload the Ring video of the theft and acknowledged receipt. She’s not expecting the thief to be caught, but figures that her report could possibly help in some way.

“I live in a pretty safe neighborhood in Amazon’s own hometown, but their delivery trucks are on our street dropping off packages every day,” she said. “It’s got to be a banquet for hungry thieves.”

She reached out to her neighbors to tell them about the theft, and one reported that she, too, had had a package stolen a week earlier.

Cooper says she did not intentionally choose the early-morning drop-off time, but it was the only time Amazon offered for her delivery. Since then, she’s seen Amazon try to offer that same time and has chosen not to order an item rather than be forced to use that dark, quiet delivery slot.

Immediately after the theft, Amazon was less than helpful, routing her to an AI agent who said it understood the situation was upsetting but that it wouldn’t be able to do anything for four days. When she checked back, Amazon agreed to refund her for the item, but kept insisting on labeling the package as “missing” and asked her to report back if she “found” it.

“I hope the driver doesn’t get in trouble for a supposedly ‘missing’ package,” she said. “It unnerves me that she was being followed by a thief. Who knows how long he followed that truck and how many packages he scooped up?”

#3015. 1Password confirms security incident, here’s what you need to know

Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its users, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

According to the company, the incident began on November 19, when it started investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The company noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our users,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That said, the company confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The company also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Finally, 1Password said users do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

#3013. I’ve tested countless Linux distros, and Pond is unlike anything I’ve tried – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Feeling adventurous? This Linux distribution is exciting, efficient and totally unique.

Linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

So too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this new take on the OS is the epitome of that.

The distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with new ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”

The developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend

If you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:

Pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind

At the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a new workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:

Once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

As I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One issue that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI update system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:

I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an update component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux

It would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

You should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my new favorite free productivity suite

Pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

#3011. Zelda Producers: Ocarina of Time Remake Is a Bridge to the Future

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Nintendo’s execs on how young designers reinterpreted a classic game, maximized the Switch 2’s graphics capabilities and briefly considered turning the Joy-Con into an ocarina.

Over the last month, I fell in love with a new game that’s actually old. It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way. How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played? And why is it still winning me over, even with Grand Theft Auto 6 here?

I’m still thinking about (and playing) Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, even with GTA 6 loaded up at home. GTA’s universe overwhelms me, but it also makes me appreciate Ocarina’s focus and clarity. And it’s also another incredible graphics showcase for what the Switch 2 is capable of. Yes, GTA 6 is jaw-dropping. But so are Ocarina’s 60fps vistas and details. Zelda pioneered 3D gaming before GTA ever went 3D.

I also can’t stop thinking about what a game like this means for Nintendo’s next wave of Switch 2 games, and a future Zelda game. Zelda’s previous games became increasingly open world, full of multiplying tasks and larger maps. It can get overwhelming. Ocarina of Time’s focus is smaller, but still tangled and immersive. Can the two concepts feed off each other? Will Ocarina help rethink where the next Zeldas are heading? And, maybe, where other open-world games are heading, too?

At Ocarina’s launch, I met in person with Nintendo’s producers for the remake, Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, to discuss what it all meant and how the remake bridged the gap between the “old Zelda” and “new Zelda.” Aonuma has been a producer for Zelda games since the original Ocarina of Time, and Fujibayashi directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

For this project, they brought on staffers who’d worked on Tears of the Kingdom, many of them much younger developers.

“In fact, some of them hadn’t even played the original Ocarina of Time on Nintendo 64,” says Aonuma. “We also saw this as a really interesting opportunity for this younger staff to make discoveries on the course of this project that they could bring forward on future Zelda projects that they might work on as well.”

There are a lot more subtle visual clues, I found, even than what I remembered in Nintendo’s last two Zelda games.

“When we were working on Tears of the Kingdom, we had this very high capacity to express all kinds of details and this feeling of immersion in the world, and that’s something I think was a big influence on the remake,” says Aonuma. “Whether it’s a visual detail that you might spot from a distance that you may not have in the original, that could be something that draws the player in and suddenly gives them the motivation to explore.”

What worked wonders, I found, was the quiet, subtle immersion, especially when exploring dungeons or figuring out solutions I’d forgotten decades ago. I had to study the environment for clues.

That’s the magic ingredient: a throughline in the Zelda games that Fujibayashi says is “the idea of exploration and discovery.”

Fujibayashi appreciates how the visual tools have improved, even since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the original Switch.

“A system that lets you share a high, dense volume of information visually provides new ways of giving clues to the player: They can use their sight to gather the information they need to do some of the puzzle solving,” he says. “Even if you compare the graphics to Breath of the Wild, it looks slightly more realistic now. And that impacts how we approach puzzle solving and puzzle creation.”

I think about Grand Theft Auto as the new benchmark for immersion and graphic detail, but I’m also finding that a lot of GTA’s discoveries are made through pop-up interaction graphics that let you know when something can be activated. Ocarina of Time doesn’t always do this. And I also can’t help but wonder: Could the Switch 2 achieve a way to run a new wave of impressive games using optimized graphics, even something on a level like Grand Theft Auto’s latest?

Or, rather, what if Nintendo aims for a new level of hyper-immersion in its games going forward, learning from Ocarina of Time?

Speaking of immersion, I kind of wish I could hold my Joy-Con up and use it like an ocarina in the new game. You can’t, although you can use the controllers to play notes or hum or play a tune into the built-in microphone using your own voice or instrument — something lots of people have been showing off online. But the Joy-Con-as-ocarina idea almost became a reality.

“To be honest, we did briefly think about doing exactly that, but then we also considered how difficult it is to turn the Joy-Con into something that’s going to make a sound that is faithful, and then also how to develop that into the application inside of the game as well,” says Aonuma. “What we ultimately decided to do instead was to have this audio recognition feature in the software where you can use any instrument that you would like, whether it’s analog or digital, and you can play these themes and have the effect in the game and experience that way.”

What I’m really hoping for is a Majora’s Mask remake, the second N64 Zelda game that built off Ocarina’s graphics engine. Nintendo could do the same here, although Nintendo wouldn’t answer my questions about Majora’s Mask during my interview.

I’m still unlocking all the little secrets in Ocarina of Time, sinking into the world as I go. And when I play the notes on my Switch, I imagine I’m playing that ocarina. After playing this Zelda game, I wonder what Nintendo could do with that same level of detail for Mario’s return on the Switch 2, almost 10 years after the last new 3D Mario game on the Switch. We might know the answer to that soon enough.

#3010. Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse said the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

#3008. Wispr Flow improves dictation accuracy with new Canto-2 speech-to-text model

Popular AI dictation app Wispr Flow is rolling out a new speech-to-text model for Mac, iPhone, and other platforms, promising fewer transcription errors and better recognition of names and technical terms. Here are the details.

Wispr Flow this week launched Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the company says reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

In practice, that means the average error rate dropped from 9.9% to 6.3% across the 14 languages, and from 3.2% to 2.7% in English, according to Wispr’s internal benchmarks.

According to the company, teaching a model to recognize specific names and terms comes with a trade-off: the more it relies on that user-specific context, the more likely it is to insert those words even when they weren’t actually spoken.

Wispr notes that Canto-2 strikes a better balance between context and accuracy, improving its ability to recognize user-specific terms without substantially increasing the frequency of incorrect substitutions:

Canto-2 recovers hard names and terms accurately nearly 7 of 10 times, without more false insertions. It makes a third fewer mistakes across 14 languages, and has the lowest Hindi error rate of any multilingual model on Hugging Face’s open benchmark. It is 10 times the scale of Canto-1, and our biggest step yet toward dictation that’s ready to send without a single edit.

According to the company, the percentage of difficult names and terms correctly recognized went from 41% to 69% between Canto-1 and Canto-2, “without inserting them more often.” It added that this improvement holds up even as the user’s custom dictionary grows, with the new model correctly recognizing 92% of easier terms even with 1,000 saved entries.

Wispr also noted that it trained Canto-2 to handle real-world dictation conditions, including background noise, laptop and phone microphones, and sentences that restart halfway through, rather than relying solely on clean recordings of scripted speech.

When tested using Hugging Face’s public multilingual benchmark, Canto-2 achieved results that would have placed it third overall as of November 9. However, Wispr conducted the evaluation itself, and the model has not yet been officially added to the leaderboard as of today, November 25.

In its own internal benchmarks, the company says Canto-2 achieved the lowest average error rate among the competing models it tested across 14 languages.

Canto-2 is now available to Wispr Flow users on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android in the Americas, with the rollout to other regions underway.

Imagine creating your own budgeting app, meal planner or productivity tool by just describing what you want. Now imagine opening that app directly from your computer without digging through your chat history.

That's exactly what Anthropic is making possible with its latest Claude update. The company announced on Tuesday that users can now turn Claude Artifacts into desktop apps for Mac and Windows, complete with their own icons, dedicated windows, and notifications.

Download or update the Claude desktop app for Mac or Windows.

Describe the app you want Claude to build.

Try out the resulting Artifact and ask Claude to make any necessary changes.

There are several limitations to keep in mind. These apps aren't completely independent of Claude. You'll need an internet connection and an active Claude login to open them, and any AI requests they make count toward your existing usage limits.

Security is another consideration. Anthropic doesn't review apps before installation, and certain permissions can let an app modify or delete files on your computer.

I'd recommend sticking with the default permissions unless your app genuinely needs additional access. Be especially careful about installing creations shared by others.

One of the things I find most compelling about this update is that it gives everyday users a reason to experiment with vibe coding beyond the novelty of building something with AI.

We don’t usually see companies announcing brand-new products just before Black Friday sales kick off, but after spending a day playing with Kodak’s new SlideTag, I’m sure glad it’s available now, because this is what most of my family is getting as a gift this year. Strictly speaking, it’s not even discounted, but its already cheap $35 price tag means this is just too good to pass up.

The SlideTag is a tiny digital photo frame that sits on a keychain, but it’s also a tracker compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub. You can load it up with photos and have the six-color E-Ink display cycle through them at set intervals, or you can put something more practical on the screen.

The Kodak app makes it easy to generate a QR code, display a to-do list, countdown to a special event or just show you the current date in a nice calendar display. It’s incredibly easy to use, the color E-Ink display is surprisingly good and setting up the tracking feature is super easy. This thing does exactly what it says it does, and with very little learning curve.

So what’s the catch? You don’t really get to choose what the outside of your SlideTag looks like. These clever little photo frames are only available as a blind box, showcasing eight designs across the vibrant history of Kodak’s packaging and something Kodak calls a secret edition, which is unique to this set.

I ordered two, and while both designs I found in the packaging are great, there are other designs in the lineup I’d have chosen first. Some retailers are selling cases of eight SlideTags with promotional packaging, like you’d see at the checkout counter of a grocery store, but this case doesn’t guarantee you’re going to get all eight designs. There’s no real way to know what you’re going to get.

That level of risk may not be your thing, but if you’re looking for a way to add a stealthy little tracker with no shortage of personality to your bag, backpack or purse, I think this is a great option. It also makes a great little gift, perfect for a stocking or white elephant party. And if this level of cutesy fun isn’t your thing, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for $18 this week.

#3004. Stock Market Today, Nov. 25: Dow Erases 1,100-Point Loss as Wall Street Stages Dramatic Late-Day Comeback

Markets recovered from steep intraday losses as investors returned to select sectors, although persistent inflation and continued weakness in technology stocks left the broader market under pressure.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 25, 2026 at 4:57PM EST

Wall Street staged a strong comeback on Wednesday, November 25, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +0.33%) erased an intraday decline of more than 1,100 points to finish in positive territory. The reversal followed another volatile session marked by persistent inflation concerns and continued selling pressure across technology stocks, highlighting a growing divergence between sectors.

The Dow climbed 0.33% to close at 50,183, outperforming the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%), which declined 0.21% to 7,186. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.62%) fell 0.62% to 23,586 as weakness in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks continued to weigh on the technology-heavy index.

Elsewhere, gold edged 0.29% higher to $3,572.40, while the 10-year Treasury yield declined slightly to 4.91%. Energy stocks led sector gains, while consumer discretionary and technology shares remained under pressure.

HP Inc. (HPQ +11.49%) surged 11.49% following better-than-expected quarterly earnings and an encouraging outlook for fiscal 2027. Charter Communications (CHTR +8.39%) also outperformed the broader market, climbing 8.39% as investors gravitated toward more defensive sectors.

Meanwhile, technology stocks continued to face substantial selling pressure. Ambarella (AMBA -19.77%) plunged 19.77% following disappointing revenue guidance, while Nutanix (NTNX -15.19%) tumbled 15.17% amid broader weakness in high-growth technology stocks.

Wednesday's dramatic market reversal suggests investors are becoming increasingly selective rather than abandoning equities altogether. Despite the Dow's recovery, continued weakness in technology stocks indicates that concerns surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) spending, elevated valuations, and the profitability of major infrastructure investments have yet to subside.

Adding to these concerns, October's core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month. Although consumer demand remains relatively resilient, persistent inflation and renewed tariff uncertainty could complicate the Federal Reserve's ability to lower interest rates. This presents a particular challenge for high-growth companies whose valuations depend heavily on expectations of future earnings.

Nevertheless, the broader market outlook is not entirely negative. Bank of America (BAC -0.04%) strategists have projected that the S&P 500 could reach 7,800 by late 2027, reflecting expectations for continued earnings growth despite near-term volatility. However, achieving that target will likely require corporate profits to expand beyond a relatively narrow group of technology companies.

Looking ahead, investors should pay particular attention to whether the rotation into other sectors can sustain the broader market while technology stocks stabilize. A recovery supported by stronger market breadth and improving earnings expectations would be more encouraging than another short-lived rally driven primarily by AI stocks.

#3003. Apple pulls popular Chinese AI chatbot from the App Store amid child safety concerns

Following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In 2023, the Shanghai-based company released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active users across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles users’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

Ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, new downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after users exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the company’s plans to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

With MSRPs of $549, $449, and $459, respectively, the Apple AirPods Max 2, Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2nd Gen, and the Sony WH-1000XM6 aren't exactly cheap. That's why Black Friday deals are so great, as they're all on sale right now.

I've tested all three of these headphones — and a boatload more of their closest competitors — so I can help you choose the correct pair. Do you value sound quality? ANC? Comfort? Extra features?

I'll go through everything the AirPods Max 2, Bose QC Ultra, and Sony XM6 offer right now — let's figure this out together. Which headphones should you buy this Black Friday?

If you're an Apple user, there are no better headphones than the AirPods Max 2 (at this price, of course). With gorgeously detailed sound and an expansive soundscape, I'm happy to overlook the slightly heavy head-feel.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra are ideal headphones if you value comfort and ANC over anything else — or, of course, if you have a predilection for bass. These headphones don't sound as detailed as Apple or Sony's versions, but they pack a major punch.

Sony's WH-1000XM6 are great headphones for most people, with clear call quality, proficient ANC, and detailed sound. They're the best all-rounder for both iPhone and Android users.

We've reached the point with Bluetooth headphones where you're probably not going to be disappointed by any pair. I've tested super-budget options worthy of making a "best of" list (Soundcore Space 2, CMF by Nothing Headphone Pro, both $99), just as I've tested these three behemoths.

There's no one "best": it all depends on your personal preferences. For the purpose of this article, I re-tested all three headphones with three of my go-to testing tracks.

The AirPods Max 2 have the most dynamic and exciting sound quality. "space cadet" by sim0ne is an energetic hard house track with euphoric '90s pianos and expansive hi-hats layered under a pitched-up female vocal. The tick-tock synths tinkled in the background with energy and zeal, while the kick drum pummelled the low-end with control.

Rock also sounds excellent on the AirPods Max 2; "Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" by Deftones starts with a grating guitar, which came through dynamically on the Max 2. The crashing cymbals at the top of the soundstage didn't wash out the grunge instrumentation, and although I can see the percussion growing tiresome after a long listening session, there's vibrancy in the soundscape.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

"Vogue (Q-Sound Mix" by Madonna is excellent for testing spatial imaging. On the AirPods Max 2, Madonna's vocals came through in each earcup independently, with no warping or confusion in the stereo. The subtle synth bassline rounded out the track delicately, without overwhelming the mids or vocals.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2nd Gen are more for bassheads. If you really like a punchy, propulsive low-end, I'd recommend the Bose.

I tested the Bose QC Ultra with the same three songs as the AirPods Max 2. "space cadet" by sim0ne wasn't as expansive or detailed as the AirPods, but the kick drum hit so much harder. As soon as the chorus broke, the synth bassline and drum machine took control of the track. The bass pulsed in my ears. sim0ne's pitched-up vocals were still clear, but the bass was the true star of the show.

"Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" benefited from the same elevated bass — the crunchy, almost too-sharp opening guitar gave way to a truly raucous verse. The bass carried the entire track, somewhat pushing the percussion to the soundstage's edge, but didn't overpower the vocals. Anyone into rock or grunge would seriously love these headphones.

Lastly, I played "Vogue (Q-Symphony Mix)" to test stereo imaging. Bose's "Immersive" feature really came into play here: I could hear the track coming from behind me, beside me, in front of me. I'd say this immersion was even better than the AirPods Max 2's — my brain was well and truly tricked. And when that bassline came in? I'm gone. It's over. I'm on the dancefloor, bye!

Last but certainly not least, let's chat about the Sony WH-1000XM6. These are famous the best "all-rounder" headphones: they're detailed and expansive, bassy yet clear, and are the best of all worlds.

Once again, I played "space cadet" by sim0ne. This track was bright and fun, with a whole load of clarity across the treble and mid-range. Every snare and hi-hat coruscated across the soundstage without overpowering those lovely tick-tock synth notes. The euphoric pianos were lovely and detailed, and when the bassline kicked in, it kicked in. Obviously, it wasn't as hard-hitting as the Bose, but the XM6s prioritize clarity and detail over booming bass.

Heavier genres fared well, too. "Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" by Deftones pounded through the headphones with the ferocity of a runaway freight train. Bass and guitars snarled in my ears without overpowering the vocals. Although the bass, again, didn't have quite as much boom as the Bose headphones, these are detail-focused instead.

Finally, I played "Vogue (Q-Symphony Mix)" to test spatial imaging. Madonna's voice danced around my head, making me feel like the music was coming from everywhere. Fingers snapped in my left ear, and bongos drummed in my right ear. I will say the Sonys weren't as truly immersive as the Bose and AirPods, but this was still a phenomenal performance.

The AirPods Max 2 are 13 ounces; Bose QC Ultra 9.3 ounces; Sony WX6 8.96 ounces. If you're going to be wearing your headphones all day, I'd recommend the Bose or Sony.

Although I can wear the AirPods Max 2 for at least a few hours without needing to take them off, and the mesh headband alleviates a lot of weight, if you need as little head fatigue as possible, I'd go for the Bose or Sony.

Especially if you're a frequent flyer — the Bose QC Ultra are unbeatable for flights. You won't be able to hear the engine, other passengers, or even your own thoughts with these. It's a win all round.

You won't be disappointed by ANC on any of these headphones. I've worn all three while working, running errands across the city, and in noisy environments like bars.

If you're wearing these headphones while working in an office, all three will minimize ambient sounds like keyboards clacking and mice clicking. I found the best to be the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, but the AirPods and Sony also cocooned me in a vacuum of quiet.

For really loud environments, or if you have noisy neighbors or construction outside your house, I'd recommend the Bose QuietComfort Ultra. While the AirPods Max 2 and Sony WH-1000XM6 are excellent, Dr. Bose literally invented ANC — and it shows.

If you want even more information, I have a full Apple AirPods Max 2 vs Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen vs Sony WH-1000XM6 for your reading pleasure.

Sony's WH-1000XM6 are great headphones for most people, with clear call quality, proficient ANC, and detailed sound. They're the best all-rounder for both iPhone and Android users.

For most people, I would recommend the Sony WH-1000XM6.

For bass lovers or frequent travelers, I'd go for the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen.

For iPhone users who value dynamic sound, grab the Apple AirPods Max 2.
