#2976. CoreWeave Stock Could Soar 125%, According to One Wall Street Analyst, Even After a Price Target Cut. Is It a Buy?

Two analysts just trimmed their CoreWeave targets but stayed bullish. The company's bonds are sending a more cautious message.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 25, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

10 stocks we like better than CoreWeave ›

CoreWeave (CRWV -0.08%) has had a brutal month. The AI cloud provider, which rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to tech giants, closed at $39.51 on Nov. 20, below its $40 IPO price from March 2025. It briefly rebounded above $48 on Monday, then gave most of that back. At about $42.57 as of Wednesday's market close, the stock is down roughly 70% from its 52-week high of $138.25 and down nearly 77% from its all-time closing high.

Wall Street analysts, meanwhile, are lowering their expectations, but not by much, and the gap between the bulls and the market is the crux of the debate.

Cantor Fitzgerald on Wednesday lowered its price target to $96 from $100 and kept its overweight rating. The firm said fears about CoreWeave's business model "continue to be overblown" and told clients to "be thankful for the discount the market has given them." Cantor said the cut reflects a higher expected share count, because raising equity at a lower stock price means issuing more shares.

A day earlier, Evercore ISI cut its target to $80 from $100 and kept its outperform rating. The analyst said the sharp correction in AI stocks has put more focus on pricing and downside risks, and assessed where the sell-off "might have overextended."

From Wednesday's closing price, Cantor's target implies upside of about 125%, and Evercore's implies about 89%.

CoreWeave's lenders are far less relaxed. Its notes due October 2031 fell nearly 2 cents to about 74 cents on the dollar on Wednesday, pushing their yield to 17.91%, Reuters reported, citing Tradeweb data. Its notes due June 2030 fell to a record low of 76.55 cents. The cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt against default has also climbed to levels usually seen at distressed companies.

A yield near 18% is a warning sign. It means lenders are demanding a return closer to what you'd expect from a stock, and bondholders get paid before shareholders. CoreWeave does have a cheaper way to borrow: its banks are preparing to sell a $4.5 billion loan backed by chips it is installing for Meta Platforms (META +3.40%) as soon as next week, Bloomberg reported. Because Meta is the customer, that loan is expected to be rated investment-grade and priced around 7% to 7.5%. But that kind of financing only works for capacity tied to a specific customer contract, not for the company as a whole.

Even Cantor concedes the market is "extremely focused" on one issue: CoreWeave's need for as much as $5 billion of "parent capital" in 2027, meaning money raised at the company level to support its build-out. Cantor thinks management should address the funding plan "sooner rather than later" and said a clear answer could act as a "potential clearing event" for the stock.

That's the crux. If CoreWeave raises capital through new shares at today's prices, existing shareholders are diluted. If it borrows, it pays rates the bond market has just pushed sharply higher. Either route makes it harder to reach the upside in those price targets.

For most investors, not yet. The analysts may well be right that the sell-off overshot, and Cantor says its review of how CoreWeave resigns customer contracts gives it more confidence in the model. But when the company's own bonds yield nearly 18%, the market is pricing in real risk that shareholders would absorb first.

Risk-tolerant investors who believe in long-term AI demand could start a small position, but the smarter move is to wait for the 2027 funding plan Cantor is asking for. If management lays out a credible way to raise that money without heavy dilution, the stock could rerate quickly. Until then, there are less leveraged ways to own the AI build-out among cloud stocks and semiconductor stocks.

Anthropic's new 'install as app' feature makes it easy to turn your Claude artifacts into desktop apps on your computer - with some limitations.

Anthropic is making its Claude artifacts available as desktop apps, meaning you can share and more easily access your most-repeated tasks on your computer. The “install as app” feature is available in beta for all free and paid Claude plans and works on both Mac and Windows, but not Linux.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Anthropic first released artifacts in 2024. Since then, they’ve become a way to standardize and repeat tasks users do regularly, especially at work. Previously, artifacts ran via your Claude window or in a browser. By splicing them out as distinct desktop apps, you can now run different Claude queries while also using your artifacts locally, or use those apps without opening Claude at all.

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer,” Anthropic said.

Artifact apps can still access Claude and any connectors you’re using, and they update automatically when you edit the artifact itself in Claude. When apps request something from Claude, though, that goes toward your Claude usage limits, which are lowest for free users.

Anthropic said the app feature is meant to streamline building apps for both developer and non-developer work.

Also: Can AI plan terrorist attacks? US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok

The update clarifies where AI software for work is headed. Claude is already more of an AI-powered work suite than a single helpful chatbot for many organizations. Evidently, people are using tools like artifacts frequently enough — and simultaneously with other Claude features — that they need those Claude-based tools to function like discrete bits of software on their own.

“If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” Anthropic said.

Claude artifact apps don’t have the same functionality as apps you could build using Claude Code, though. Even if you don’t need Claude open for these apps to work, you’ll still need to be signed in to Claude and have internet access, so they’re not an entirely portable or off-grid option.

The feature’s support page also notes that legacy artifacts, “live artifacts from Claude Cowork,” and artifacts generated from templates like Docs, Slides, and Sheets can’t be installed as desktop apps.

First, make sure Claude for Mac or Windows is updated. You can try the “install as app” feature, which is in beta for all free and paid plans, via Claude’s Share menu. Select the Install as app option, which will then download the artifact you chose to your desktop. From there, set permissions as needed.

Permissions range from the default (whatever they are in a browser) to app-specific permissions like sending notifications and full computer access.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Full computer access means the artifact app can “run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time,” Anthropic said, so proceed carefully. Every time you edit and update the artifact (and thus the app), Claude will ask you to confirm permissions again, so you’ll ideally have regular checkpoints to revise access. Still, there are some guardrails in place: Anthropic only lets you give full computer access to apps you’ve made yourself. For Team and Enterprise plans, that extends to any apps made by your coworkers.

“Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust,” the company said.

For Claude Enterprise plans, the install-as-app feature is off entirely until an admin turns it on in Organization settings.

#2973. What Are Repositioning Cruises?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#2972. The Winter Solstice Is Coming: A Guide to the Longest Night

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Next month, we'll experience the shortest daylight hours of the year.

This was taken with the main camera as a ProRaw photo. Notice the lights on the tree, compared to the green hue of the street lighting and blue and pink tones in the sky.

Thanksgiving is almost here, as is Cyber Monday, but soon it’ll be officially winter. The winter solstice is on Dec. 21, when we’ll experience Earth’s shortest, darkest day.

The winter solstice has a few different meanings, so here are all of them. The most common definition, and the one you’re most likely familiar with, is that it denotes the shortest day and longest night of the year on Earth. These times vary depending on your location on the globe, but the further north you live, the less sunlight you’ll get. In the tropics, they’ll get about 12 hours of sunlight. In Sweden, it’ll be closer to 6 hours. In Svalbard, there isn’t any.

The reason this occurs is due to the second definition of the winter solstice: During this time, the North Pole is tilted as far away from the sun as it can get. According to The Farmer’s Almanac, the moment at which the Earth’s axis is physically tilted as much as it can be is at 3:50 p.m. ET on Monday, Dec. 21. After that moment, the process will begin to reverse until the South Pole takes its turn during the summer solstice. At that point, the North Pole will be at its closest tilt to the sun, giving us the longest day and shortest night of the year for the Northern Hemisphere.

Sunset will occur at its earliest time on Dec. 21.

It’ll vary by location. The southern US will have the most sunlight, with Florida getting a little over 10 hours during the winter solstice. The Midwest and Great Lakes portion of the country will get roughly nine hours. The Pacific Northwest can expect a little less than nine hours. Southern Alaska will get about six hours, and the northern areas of Alaska will see around three hours.

If you want to see how your area will fare, Time and Date has a sunrise and sunset tool you can use. Input your zip code into the search bar, and you’ll be able to see your sunrise and sunset times.

The city of Utqiaġvik, Alaska, will have it worse than most in the US: It won’t get any sun at all. The sun won’t rise there again until late January. We hope the people living there packed their vitamin D supplements.

The autumn equinox was just a couple of months ago, so you may be curious about the differences. A solstice occurs when the Earth’s poles are tilted as far away from the sun as they’ll be over the course of one year, which is also one orbit around the sun. The equinoxes take place at the halfway points between each solstice. The autumn equinox takes place in September between the summer and winter solstices, while the spring equinox takes place in March between the winter and summer.

During an equinox, the poles are minimally tilted, and the days are as even as they can be. This also has a couple of other interesting side effects: The sun is pointed directly at the equator during an equinox, and the sun will rise and set directly east and west, respectively.

Humans use the solstices and equinoxes to mark the change of the seasons. There are two equinoxes and two solstices, which mark the start and end dates for Earth’s four seasons.

Decorating with evergreen trees, like with a wreath, is what they used to do to celebrate the winter solstice.

While the solstice is close to the holidays, celebrations for the winter solstice have been around for significantly longer, and some winter solstice traditions have become Christmas traditions as well. One of the most historically famous winter solstice celebrations is Yule, a winter festival originating thousands of years ago among the ancient Norse. It became commonly celebrated in Europe and involved bonfires and massive feasts. Yule celebrations also included decorating with evergreen tree decorations, like holly and ivy.

If these sound familiar, it’s because Christmas co-opted many of those traditions centuries ago, and the two traditions have kind of merged into a single seasonal holiday. The terms Yule and Christmas are often used interchangeably these days in many cultures.

So if you want to celebrate the winter solstice, just do all of the stuff you would normally do for the holidays. Burn a Yule log, decorate a tree, eat a big feast with your family and hang up mistletoe and wreaths — those are all hat tips to traditional winter solstice celebrations.

Meanwhile, lowering prices has, indeed, hurt revenues and earnings. But the company upped its full-year 2026 guidance when it reported third-quarter 2026 earnings. That suggests that the volume-led transition is going well.

Novo Nordisk's 4.4% yield is historically high and well above the pharmaceutical industry average of 1.3%. Its roughly 10x price-to-earnings ratio is also well below the industry average of 27x. It looks like a bargain for more aggressive income investors, and a $1,000 investment will net you roughly 24 shares.

PepsiCo is one of the world's largest consumer staples companies. It is an industry leader in the snack and beverage areas, and it has a sizable packaged food business as well. It is more diversified than most of its peers, and it can stand toe-to-toe with any of them as a business, with strong brands, marketing, innovation, and distribution.

The problem is that PepsiCo's business isn't firing on all cylinders right now, with its organic sales growth notably lagging that of key peer Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%). Still, PepsiCo's 3.1% organic sales growth in the third quarter wasn't bad, even though it was less than half of Coca-Cola's 7%. But investors remain worried, thanks notably to weakness in PepsiCo's large U.S. operations.

That's fair, but PepsiCo is a Dividend King, with over 50 annual dividend increases. It has been through difficult times before and survived. And it is making the types of decisions you would expect during the current difficult period, including acquiring desirable brands and introducing innovative new products. It is highly likely that the company will get through this and thrive again over the long term.

If you buy it now, however, you get to collect the historically high 4.1% yield. And you are buying it while its 18x P/E is notably below its 25x five-year average. For reference, the average consumer staples stock yields 2% and has a P/E of around 26x. A $1k investment will buy roughly seven PepsiCo shares.

To be fair, neither Novo Nordisk nor PepsiCo is about to suddenly break out of their funk. So you have to go in with a long-term mindset. However, you'll get to collect a well above-market income stream while you wait for these historically well-run businesses to get back on track. And given their recent performance and historical results, it seems highly likely that they will eventually do just that.

#2970. Fast Fashion Fiasco: Shein to Pay $100 Million in FTC Complaint

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The company agrees to the fine after the FTC alleged it deceived US customers.

Shein, one of the biggest fast-fashion brands in the world, has been ordered to pay $100 million by the Federal Trade Commission, which alleges that the Singapore-based online retail giant engaged in deceptive practices that left millions of US customers dissatisfied with its products and policies.

The FTC complaint alleges that Shein failed to follow through on its swift shipping policies, made it difficult for customers to resolve purchase issues and stifled negative customer reviews from seeing the light of day.

The complaint also alleges problems with the company’s supply chain, false information about the origin of the cotton used in its clothes, a failure to communicate shipping updates to customers and a lack of support for those whose packages were late or went missing altogether.

“The company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Shein has ballooned over the past decade into the ultra-fast-fashion brand we know today, thanks in large part to the impact influencers have had on social media, posting videos trying on clothing supplied by the company.

In 2026, the company is estimated to ship roughly 1 million packages to US customers daily, according to the FTC. That number becomes even more astounding when you consider that Shein, the FTC alleges, employed just five customer service agents to answer calls from American customers.

This isn’t the first time Shein has faced negative scrutiny. Over the years, the company has faced allegations of numerous workers’ rights violations and is the largest polluter in the fast-fashion industry.

According to Yale Climate Connections, the company emitted 16.7 million total metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere in 2023. Comparatively speaking, that’s more than the pollution output of four coal power plants. Shein has since pledged to improve its treatment of workers and reduce carbon emissions, but scrutiny persists.

The $100 million will be used to compensate customers. And according to the FTC’s proposed order, the company, which earned roughly $50 billion in revenue in 2025, will not be able to continue advertising inaccurate shipping and delivery times; negative reviews will no longer be hidden; and its customer service offering will be bolstered.

“The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC’s characterization of our business and compliance practices,” a Shein spokesperson told CNET.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#2967. The Nvidia Scandal Set Off a Chip Crackdown in Congress. Which Stocks Are Most at Risk?

Congress is moving toward sweeping new chip export controls. One research firm says the biggest loser may not be an American company at all.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 25, 2026 at 5:58PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) has spent November at the center of a political storm, with Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO amid allegations that its chips were smuggled into China. The stock fell another 4% on Wednesday. But the company most at risk from Washington's response may be one most investors don't connect to the scandal at all.

In a note published Wednesday, research firm TS Lombard said the Nvidia fallout has galvanized lawmakers, putting Congress on track to pass three to four new chip export-control measures, most likely as part of the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. Grace Fan, the firm's managing director of global policy and disruptive themes research, said passage is a question of "when" and not "if," though a government shutdown fight around the Dec. 11 funding deadline could push it into early 2027.

The bills would close several loopholes at once. One would give Congress a say over exports of the most advanced AI chips. Another would require location tracking on exported AI chips to stop smuggling. A third would target Chinese companies renting U.S. chips through overseas cloud services. The centerpiece, the MATCH Act, goes after the machines that make chips rather than the chips themselves.

The MATCH Act would pressure U.S. allies, mainly the Netherlands and Japan, to match U.S. restrictions on the sale of chipmaking equipment to China. If they don't, TS Lombard said, the Senate version would direct the Commerce Department to impose the controls itself after about 150 days. The Senate bill also names every deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machine among the tools that couldn't go to China at all.

That's why TS Lombard says the companies most at risk aren't U.S. equipment makers such as Applied Materials (AMAT -3.89%), Lam Research (LRCX -5.68%), and KLA (KLAC +0.41%), which already face U.S. rules. Instead, it points to ASML (ASML -2.47%), the Dutch lithography leader, and Japan's Tokyo Electron, along with several other Japanese suppliers. The Dutch government has said it opposes the bill.

Wednesday's trading didn't reflect that ranking. Lam fell 6% and Applied Materials 4%, while ASML dropped 2.5% to about $1,303, roughly 35% below its 52-week high.

There are two reasons ASML's exposure is shrinking. TS Lombard estimates that China will account for about 20% of ASML's sales this year, down from roughly 30% in fiscal 2025. Chinese chipmakers also front-loaded their purchases, building what the firm estimates is about three years' worth of DUV machines.

That stockpile cuts both ways. It means fewer new China orders were coming anyway, but it shifts the fight to servicing and spare parts, which the Senate version would also restrict. TS Lombard expects China to retaliate in measured ways, possibly by squeezing Dutch and Japanese companies, and sees a likely middle path in which some servicing licenses are traded for access to critical minerals.

For long-term investors, yes, if you buy gradually. ASML is the only company that makes the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines needed for the most advanced chips, and that position doesn't depend on China. A smaller China business is a hit to near-term sales, not to its long-term moat.

The near-term risk is real, though. Headlines on the defense bill, the Dec. 11 funding deadline, and the Trump-Xi meeting at the G20 summit in Miami on Dec. 14-15 could all move the shares. Investors who want exposure to semiconductor stocks can use that volatility to build a position in stages rather than all at once, and keep an eye on Tokyo Electron and other tech stocks with heavy China exposure as the bill takes shape.

#2965. 'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Just Closed His Bet Against the Nasdaq. Here's What Investors Should Do Now

The investor famous for calling the 2008 housing crash says he's now "temporarily almost entirely long." Here's how to read the move without copying it.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Palantir Technologies ›

Michael Burry made his name betting against the housing market before the 2008 financial crisis. This week, with tech stocks in a steep slide, he did something somewhat unusual for him: He stopped betting against the market.

In a post on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, Burry said he had sold the rest of his put options on the Nasdaq-100, bearish bets that pay off when the index falls. "Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," he wrote. Apart from puts on Palantir Technologies (PLTR +1.50%) and MetLife (MET +0.57%), he added, "I am temporarily almost entirely long."

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Burry is turning more bullish after a sharp drop. The Nasdaq Composite closed Tuesday at 23,733.54, down 14.5% from its Oct. 6 close, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 16% over the same stretch. The Composite is down about 7% in November alone, as doubts about whether the AI spending boom will pay off, new tariff proposals, and the turmoil around Nvidia's leadership have weighed on AI stocks.

Puts gain value as an index falls, so selling them after a slide is a way to lock in profits. Burry said much of his cash, about 25% of the portfolio, came from profitable put options plus money added to the account.

The most important word in his post may be "temporarily." Burry said he is "continuing to assess short opportunities," and he hasn't said the market has bottomed. He also kept his Palantir puts, even though Palantir shares, at about $164 on Wednesday, already sit roughly 23% below their 52-week high.

Burry disclosed large put positions on Nvidia and Palantir in late 2025 after warning about an AI bubble. Shifting from that stance to mostly long tells you he thinks a good part of the downside he expected has now played out, at least for the broad index.

For most investors, the answer is not to copy his trades. Burry can reverse a position in a day and write about it afterward, so by the time a move becomes news, he may have changed it again. Short-selling and options are tools most individual investors shouldn't rely on.

The useful lesson is in how he's behaving. He took profits on a bet that worked, he's holding a big cash cushion, and he's staying selective about what he owns. You can do a version of that: Make a list of quality tech stocks you'd be glad to own for five years, and buy them in stages if the sell-off continues, rather than all at once. Keep enough cash on the side that you're never forced to sell in a downturn.

Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday, so expect thin trading and bigger swings to end the week. If Burry's right that the worst of the Nasdaq's slide is behind it, patient buyers will be rewarded. If he's wrong, he's already told you he can switch back, and investors buying in stages will have room to do the same.

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," said Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

#2962. If SpaceX and Tesla Merge Next Year, Here's What a $5,000 Investment in the Combined Company Could Be Worth by the End of 2028

An investment in Tesla could double in the event of a Space Exploration Technologies merger.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:04PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

The odds of Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) and Tesla (TSLA -1.18%) merging sometime next year have been growing. Prediction market odds jumped earlier this month after Elon Musk's biographer, Walter Isaacson, told CNBC he was confident a merger is coming, since keeping the companies separate makes no sense. This was followed by the two companies picking board members to begin official merger talks.

Isaacson's comments raised the odds that SpaceX would announce a merger with Tesla before March 1, 2027, from 27% on Nov. 11, 2026, to 62% two days later. They now sit at 67%, as of Nov. 24 on Kalshi. Meanwhile, the odds of a merger announcement before the end of 2027 are at 89% on Polymarket.

Now, a merger isn't a foregone conclusion and does face some hurdles, but it does seem very likely at this point. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections complicate matters a bit, as Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson told Bloomberg that a potential merger would face "tremendous scrutiny." Meanwhile, more than half of all Tesla shareholders would need to vote to approve the merger, not just those who decide to vote. Musk owns nearly 20% of the company, but Tesla also has a significant retail shareholder base that would have to vote on the deal for it to pass.

Despite these obstacles, there is still a very good shot that the companies announce a merger next year and complete it by the end of 2028. In such a scenario, it would be best to purchase shares of Tesla, the acquired company. With a little over $5,000, an investor could buy around 13 shares of Tesla.

An acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX ultimately makes a lot of sense. First, it unites Musk's two largest companies and will allow him to focus on a single vision instead of splitting his time between the two. Second, the companies already have an important joint venture in the form of their massive chip manufacturing facility, Terafab, so it would make sense to have this under one roof. Finally, the companies' businesses complement each other.

More than anything, both SpaceX and Tesla are about the future, and together they give Musk and investors more shots on goal. Meanwhile, SpaceX could ultimately need some of Tesla's technology to build its planned data centers in space, including solar and Optimus robots. As such, the deal makes sense from a synergy perspective, and the company would be able to cut some overlapping corporate costs.

Any merger between SpaceX and Tesla is likely to be an all-stock deal in which Tesla is acquired at a premium. Analysts at HSBC recently pegged the most likely premium around 33% based on past similar deals, which makes sense.

Based on that premium and current prices, investors would get a little over 4 SpaceX shares for each Tesla share they hold. That would turn investors' 13 Tesla shares into 52 SpaceX shares after the merger, worth $5,000.

For a combined SpaceX-Tesla, the stock would likely trade based on a forward price-to-sales (P/S) ratio. For 2029, the Tesla revenue consensus estimate is $146 billion, while SpaceX's is roughly $336 billion. Combined, that's $482 billion in estimated annual revenue for 2029.

Place a 12-times multiple on that, given its strong growth outlook, and the combined company would be worth $5.8 trillion. Meanwhile, following the merger, it would have roughly 29.7 billion shares. That would value SpaceX at approximately $195. Those 52 shares would then be worth about $10,150, approximately double a $5,000 initial investment in two years.

This makes Tesla a top growth stock to buy ahead of a potential SpaceX merger.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

#2960. Why GDS Holdings Stock Topped the Market Today

The company posted a much narrower loss than many expected in its third quarter.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:27PM EST

10 stocks we like better than GDS Holdings ›

Tech stocks didn't do well in the last trading session before Thanksgiving. One exception was Chinese techie GDS Holdings (GDS +0.07%); its American Depositary Shares (ADSs) inched up marginally on a day when the S&P 500 index dipped by almost 0.3%. It managed to swim against the current due to its latest earnings release, which featured better-than-expected fundamentals.

GDS Holdings' third quarter saw the company reap 3.18 billion yuan ($477 million) in revenue, up 10% year over year. On the bottom line, the company flipped to a loss of 5.47 million yuan ($821 million) from the year-ago profit of 712.31 million yuan ($107 million) -- although the third-quarter 2025 figure was inflated by a one-time accounting gain of 1.37 billion yuan ($206 million). On a per-ADS basis, GDS' loss was 0.04 yuan ($0.01).

Although no investor appreciates a tumble into the red, analysts tracking GDS were expecting far worse. Their estimate for net loss was 0.24 yuan ($0.04) per ADS. The company also beat the average pundit projection of 3.14 billion yuan ($471 million) for revenue.

GDS is a company in transition, shifting from a cloud computing focus to a focus on operating artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. The company said new bookings and continued progress in getting its facilities onstream helped push revenue higher. Higher costs, primarily from data center build-outs, affected the bottom line.

In the earnings release, GDS reaffirmed its existing annual revenue and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) guidance. The former line item should come in at 12.7 billion yuan ($1.91 billion) to 13 billion yuan ($1.95 billion), which forecasts at least 11% growth over the 2025 figure. Non-GAAP (adjusted) EBITDA is estimated at 5.9 billion yuan ($885 million) to 6.1 billion yuan ($915 million).

The current pullback in AI infrastructure stocks in the U.S. market weighed on sentiment toward GDS, whose quarterly performance was actually quite encouraging. If I were an ADS holder, I'd be pleased that revenue growth is poised to accelerate, given the company's backlog and considerable committed space across its facilities.

#2959. Here’s How Many Coca-Cola Shares It Takes to Earn $1,300 Every Quarter in Dividends

You would need to own more than 2,450 shares of Coca-Cola to generate $1,300 in dividend income.

By Matthew Benjamin – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:28PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%) has been a great stock to own in 2026.

Shares of the giant beverage maker are up more than 40% year to date (compared with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%), which has risen just about 4.5% this year).

In addition to that impressive gain, Coca-Cola is also a Dividend King, a company that has raised its dividend for at least 50 consecutive years. In fact, Coke has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years.

That annual dividend currently stands at $2.12 per share, or $0.53 each quarter.

So, to earn a healthy $1,300 per quarter in dividends, how many shares would you need to own? Well, it's as simple as dividing $1,300 by 0.53.

You would need to own 2,453 shares to generate that much quarterly dividend income. That's a hefty investment: That many shares would cost $240,394 at the current share price of $98.

All that said, I believe Coca-Cola is a very good investment right now for two main reasons. First, the stock has historically held up well in recessions and bear markets. And second, while the rise of GLP-1 drugs is hurting some snack food and beverage companies, about 68% of Coca-Cola's portfolio consists of low- or no-calorie drink options.

So, you might not be able to afford enough KO shares to generate over $1,000 in income per quarter, but an investment in this stock is, in my opinion, a wise one.

#2958. Mortgage Rates Today, Wednesday, November 25: A Little Lower

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

This under-the-radar software infrastructure stock boasts a Superscore of 84 from our Hidden Gems Primary database, part of The Motley Fool's Moneyball Database system. Here's why.

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 25, 2026 at 6:29PM EST

When a large enterprise needs to update its software, it doesn't just push a button and hope for the best. It relies on a central nervous system to store, secure, and distribute those updates across thousands of servers. JFrog (FROG +0.27%) has built that system. By acting as the universal repository for software packages, it has become the invisible plumbing that powers global application delivery. The stock, which trades at $109.60 as of November 19, 2026, has gained 80% over the past year as developers increasingly lean on its platform to manage the complexity of modern, AI-integrated software supply chains.

JFrog is in a great position to grow its business over the next several years thanks to the artificial intelligence boom. AI is making it easier and faster for developers to generate code. As a result, enterprises need automated systems to store, track, and govern the resulting software packages and AI models.

This contributed to JFrog's enterprise customers signing massive, multi-year contracts resulting in a 60% year-over-year increase in Q3 cloud sales to $101.5 million. Cloud income represented 46% of revenue last year, and has grown to 57% at the end of the third quarter in a sign JFrog's enterprise moat is widening, anchored by high switching costs.

Another factor in JFrog's favor is that it bundles cybersecurity features into its platform, strengthening the safety and security of the software code it manages. This also delivers a unified "system of record" that increases contract sizes and platform stickiness, encouraging customers to consolidate their spending with JFrog.

The success of this approach is demonstrated by the company's robust net dollar retention rate of 124%, up from 118% in the previous year. As the use of AI code continues to expand, JFrog is poised for years of ongoing business expansion ahead.

#2956. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Dodge ranks No. 476 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.5%. See Brookfield Infrastructure Partners KPIs on TipRanks.

#2955. Why CleanSpark Stock Was a Winner on Wednesday

The company published its final earnings report for fiscal 2026.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 25, 2026 at 7:10PM EST

10 stocks we like better than CleanSpark ›

CleanSpark's (CLSK +1.27%) final earnings release of its current fiscal year was published after market hours on Tuesday. The following day, investors showed their somewhat cautious appreciation for the company's performance by trading its shares up by almost 1.3%. While not every metric in CleanSpark's fourth quarter was impressive, the company improved several important line items.

We can't say that for net revenue, as it declined to $120.9 million from $223.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2025. That wasn't a shock or surprise, however, as the company's legacy business of Bitcoin (BTC +2.14%) mining was affected by a drop in the crypto's average price while it was building out its artificial intelligence (AI) data center business.

The dynamic was much different on the bottom line, where CleanSpark flipped to a net profit of $9.8 million ($0.04 per share) from the year-ago loss of $925,000. Much of this, however, was tied to its legacy business -- it booked a nearly $306 million accounting gain on the value of its Bitcoin, despite the digital currency's recent softening.

This meant a mixed quarter for CleanSpark, as it whiffed on the analyst consensus estimate of $134.3 million. Yet it trounced the average pundit expectation of a $0.33 per share net loss.

The company's results are choppy due to the nature of the Bitcoin mining business, which, for obvious reasons, depends on the cryptocurrency's price. CleanSpark has now entered a pivotal fiscal year for its transformation, as it expects to begin drawing revenue from high-profile clients for AI data center space.

Given that, I'd say that investors were buying into CleanSpark based on that high-potential future rather than the unexpected flip into profitability. I'd be even more cautious than those folks. At the same time, though, AI data center operation is almost certainly a durable and lucrative business; this company isn't the only legacy crypto miner making the transition, and it hasn't yet proven it can soar above such peers.
