#2897. HP: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Margin pressure from memory chip costs and a consumer slump sits alongside a $1 billion savings target that is still ahead.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 11:10PM EST

On its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, HP (HPQ +11.49%) announced fourth-quarter revenue of $16 billion, representing 9% growth year over year. Commercial hardware demand and the adoption of artificial intelligence helped offset consumer market softness and rising component costs. HP returned over $2.3 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases in fiscal year 2026. Three takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Enterprise clients are accelerating device upgrades as local artificial intelligence (AI) processing reduces latency and keeps proprietary corporate data on-site. Demand for higher-value commercial devices and workstations lifted Personal Systems segment revenue 14% year over year.

Escalating memory chip costs and excess channel inventory pulled consumer revenue down 7% year over year, compressing Personal Systems operating margins to 3%. Management is reducing bill-of-materials costs and adjusting pricing to restore segment margins to target levels before fiscal year-end.

Declining office printing supplies volume reduced overall print segment revenue 1% year over year, but expansion in subscription services and refillable tank printers protected segment profitability. Refillable tank hardware placements increased total customer lifetime value and lifted the printing segment's operating margins above target levels.

Component inflation and soft personal computer demand create near-term friction, but structural cost reductions and expanding enterprise adoption of edge computing create a clearer path to profit recovery. Management relies on disciplined pricing, software attach, and commercial workstation growth while modernizing global supply chains.

Free cash flow generation supports consistent shareholder returns, including an 11th consecutive annual dividend increase. Enterprise customers migrating artificial intelligence tasks locally provide HP a durable structural tailwind.

#2894. Lakers star divulges ‘uncomfortable’ reason for success without Austin Reaves

For the first four weeks of the season, the Lakers, for the most part, won their games in similar fashion.

A scorching start from Luka Doncic en route to a 30-point (and oftentimes, 40-point) performance.

Austin Reaves, Doncic's backcourt co-star, efficiently filled in the gaps offensively en route to an uber-efficient 25-point game.

Walker Kessler provided the rim pressure the team needed, which in combination with the scoring/playmaking from Doncic and Reaves, opened up scoring opportunities for the players around them.

Luka Doncic #77 and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers look on. NBAE via Getty Images

Los Angeles Lakers forward Jarred Vanderbilt playing defense. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

The recipe not only led to the Lakers winning 12 of their first 14 games, but also powered them to have the league's top-ranked offense.

But then the formula that led them to most of their early-season victories changed before their longest stretch of games at home.

The ingredients changing meant the recipe for success also had to be altered – which the Lakers successfully pulled off during the 3–1 homestand that ended with Monday's victory over the Jazz.

Doncic cooled off from his sizzling start to the season during the homestand, averaging 29.5 points (38.5% shooting, 23.5% on 3-pointers), after averaging 39 points (48.6% shooting, 40.6% on 3s) beforehand.

Utah Jazz forward Kyle Filipowski (2) goes up for a basket as Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) defends. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

Reaves wasn't available, missing the last five games because of a bruised left heel. The Lakers are hopeful he'll return during Friday's road game against the Spurs.

Which led to the Lakers leaning on their defense to pull out most of their recent wins.

"We have a standard and we have to play to that standard and do what we're supposed to," Collin Sexton said. "When you're playing to a standard, it doesn't matter who's in and who's out. We all have to help. It doesn't matter who's coming into the game, we all have a role to play to do what the person in front of us did."

The Lakers held the Hornets to 114 points in their overtime win Nov. 17, allowed 109 points in the Nov. 18 loss to the Jazz, held the Kings to 104 points in Friday's win before holding the Jazz to 94 points on Monday, which is the fewest amount of points a team has scored against the Lakers this season.

Los Angeles Lakers forward Jarred Vanderbilt (2) vies for the ball against Utah Jazz forward Kyle Filipowski. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

Their halfcourt defense has been a strength of the Lakers throughout the season.

But they cleaned up some of their transition defensive concerns. They remained disruptive, recording at least 16 turnovers in each game of the homestand. And using more zone defense, sometimes with full-court pressure, gave the Lakers a boost on that end of the floor.

"We have a lot of like disruptors defensively," Jake LaRavia said. "We do a good job at just creating pressure for the other team, whether it's deflections or just ball pressure, and kind of making them uncomfortable in bringing the ball up the court. It's obviously been working for us, so we're going to keep doing it 'til it stops working."

The Lakers' defensive rating improved from No. 17 to No. 10 during the homestand – albeit against inferior opponents that have a combined record of 9–43.

They're going to need Reaves available and improved play from Doncic as the level of competition picks up with the four-game trip post-Thanksgiving that features matchups against the Spurs, Grizzlies and Rockets. Those are three of the four teams closest to the Lakers in the top of the Western Conference standings.

But even though it wasn't always pretty, the Lakers showed they can at least win in other ways outside of what they showed in the first few weeks of the season.

"Austin is a very, very important piece to this team, and so seeing how we compete without him, not at our full strength, that's good," Kessler said. "It builds resiliency. Because [you're] not going to be always [at] your full strength. Things happen, it's a long season, so it's encouraging to see."

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 11:10PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Axis Capital ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, AXIS (AXS +1.14%) announced gross written premiums rose 11% year over year to $2.4 billion. For long-term shareholders, disciplined risk selection protects underwriting margins while broader insurance pricing moderates. Expanding book value per share, the core measure of net asset growth, creates compounding potential without pushing into mispriced coverage. Three things management said stand out.

When insurance rates drop below loss costs in broad liability and property lines, writing more coverage destroys value. AXIS cut liability and cyber premiums by 8% and 14%, respectively, year to date -- primarily in reinsurance -- to shield underwriting profits, choosing to expand instead in higher-return niches like marine war risk.

Automation in specialized underwriting frees up human capacity while speeding up business execution. The company rolled out a next-generation underwriting platform that reduced quote cycle times by up to 70% for lower-middle-market accounts, accelerating growth without adding fixed overhead.

Buying back stock below intrinsic value boosts per-share net asset value faster than unneeded premium growth. Management retired 16.6% of common shares since late 2023, expanding repurchases as market pricing softened across property and casualty lines.

Rising portfolio yields drive fixed income returns higher, providing steady cash flow as primary market rates moderate. Specialty underwriting discipline and selective capital deployment maintain portfolio margins without chasing market volume.

Targeted exposure management ensures long-term compounding across shifting risk cycles.

#2887. Ambarella: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Customers are delaying orders as memory shortages persist, but Ambarella's new 2nm, 4nm, and 5nm chips are set to carry second-half fiscal 2028 growth.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 11:16PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Ambarella ›

On its third-quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 24, 2026, Ambarella (AMBA -19.77%) announced quarterly revenue of $115.2 million. Industrywide shortages of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), a type of computer memory chip, are forcing customers to delay orders and rethink product timing. Three things management said stand out.

Memory price spikes hit consumer markets hard, driving subseasonal guidance for the fourth quarter. Management pruned customer forecasts to exclude unconfirmable shipments while customers rationed available memory for high-priority products.

Management projects full-year revenue growth in fiscal 2028, propelled by new 5-nanometer, 4-nanometer, and 2-nanometer system-on-chips (SoCs) -- integrated microchips containing primary system components. These devices command a higher average selling price (ASP), or baseline unit price, than legacy products.

Ambarella added global design house Sigma Connectivity to its partner network to support complex artificial intelligence (AI) chip integrations. The company is leveraging partners to reach small and mid-sized enterprise accounts in emerging robotics and infrastructure markets.

Industrywide memory headwinds are biting, but management isn't wavering on its long-term strategy.

Ambarella holds a $22.9 billion serviceable addressable market (SAM), or total potential market revenue, for fiscal 2032. Management is scrutinizing discretionary expenses while expanding its open software platform.

#2884. Fantasy Basketball Rankings (9-cat leagues): Risers and fallers through Week 5

We're onto Week 6! Here is the 9-cat version of my risers and fallers list. These rankings are for rest-of-season 9-cat leagues, and I'm leaning on Yahoo's rankings from the last two weeks and last month. Efficiency matters more here than in points leagues, and it's the main thing separating these six players. Let's get into it!

Ausar is averaging 10.8 points, 8.7 rebounds, 5.4 assists, 1.6 steals and 1 block on 55% shooting through 16 games, and he's been even better lately. He's eighth over the last two weeks and 30th over the last month. He leads the Pistons in rebounding and had a 17-board game against Philadelphia on Nov. 4. The weak spots are well known. Those with punt-3 builds get the most out of him, since he positively adds value in rebounds, assists, stocks and field goal percentage. The jump to 73% from the line is another win, as he doesn't hurt you nearly as badly as he used to.

I have him 57th, as I anticipate Jalen Duren's return will impact his numbers to some degree. Either way, he's exceeding expectations in what could be a breakout campaign.

Smith is averaging 14.1 points, 7.5 rebounds, 2.1 3s and 1 block in 25.3 minutes, shooting 55% from the field with 0.9 turnovers per game. That mix of 3s, blocks, field goal percentage and low turnovers is why he grades out well in 9-cat without much volume. He's 14th over the last two weeks and 26th over the last month. He was drafted in just 8% of Yahoo leagues, so if you scooped him up off waivers, you're playing with house money.

I'm moving him up to 65th, from 99th, but not higher because much of this production came with Nic Claxton sidelined. Caleb Wilson is also out, and Claxton is still ramping up, so Smith's role should hold for now. I could be too low on him. Continue to hold.

McDaniels is 11th over the last two weeks and 18th over the last month.  The bump in usage comes from Anthony Edwards' absence. Edwards is out until late January after knee surgery, and McDaniels has absorbed a bigger share of the offense without losing efficiency. He's averaging 18.4 points, 6.2 rebounds, 3.7 assists, 1.2 steals, 0.9 blocks and 1.6 3s in 33.9 minutes, shooting 56% from the field and 85% from the line.

He's positive in eight of nine categories, with turnovers (2.2 per game) the only negative. I don't value turnovers that much, especially when he's so productive across other areas of fantasy. Some of that scoring should come back down when Edwards returns, which is why I have him 30th, up from 43rd. I wouldn't sell, even though his play is on another level right now.

Hart is 233rd over the last two weeks and 176th over the last month. His scoring is down to 6.6 points per game from 12.0 last season, and he's shooting 34% from the field and 60% from the line. He's still contributing 6.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists, which keeps him rosterable, but his steals have dipped recently and he's listed as questionable with a right shoulder sprain. In 9-cat, the low percentages make it a bigger problem. The good news is that his minutes appear to be trending back up. Landry Shamet's been eating into his minutes because of his shooting, but over the past two games, Hart's averaging 37 minutes per gam. He's also coming off a 10-11-10 triple-double, which could be a nice selling point if you're concerned about his ROS outlook.

I have him 120th, down from 72nd. I'd hold in 12-team 9-cat leagues for now since his shooting should improve, but he's not as bad as Mikal Bridges, who was near drop status.

Gobert is 239th over the last two weeks and 289th over the last month. His rebound and block rates are both down: he's averaging 10.6 rebounds and 1.0 block in 29.2 minutes, compared to 11.5 and 1.6 last season. His scoring has dropped from 10.9 to 7.6 points, and his field goal percentage is down to 49% after he shot 68.2% last season. That FG% was the main reason to roster him in 9-cat. He's also shooting 46% from the line on 4.7 attempts per game. That's way too much volume for someone shooting so poorly.

The former four-time defensive player of the year is more of a rebound specialist, so I'd look to move him if he can string together a few big double-double outings. I have him 150th, down from 110th. I'm probably still too generous.

Reid has the volume in his first season in Charlotte: 17.7 points, 8.3 rebounds and 2.5 3s in 31.5 minutes. The problem is efficiency. He's shooting 38% from the field on 17.5 attempts and 66% from the line, well below his career norms (45.6% and 73.2% last season in Minnesota), and he's adding 2.5 turnovers. That's why he's 149th over the last two weeks and 197th over the last month.

I have him 96th, down from 86th, because I expect his percentages to rebound once the Hornets get healthier and he isn't carrying as much of the offense. The volume makes him an easier hold in points leagues, but fantasy managers have every right to be concerned about his numbers.

#2879. Central Garden & Pet: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Central is swapping low-margin channels for recognized brands like Burpee and TRIXIE, but seasonal Burpee losses and elevated retailer inventory will weigh on the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 11:22PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Central Garden & Pet ›

On its fourth quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 23, 2026, Central Garden & Pet (CENT -7.59%) announced full-year non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share of $3.27 alongside guidance of $2.65 or better for fiscal 2027. Investors tracking the business need to evaluate how management's strategic portfolio pruning and brand acquisitions support profit margins amid fluctuating consumer demand. Three key takeaways from management's comments stand out.

Central Garden & Pet is leaning into corporate acquisitions to replace divested lower-margin distribution channels with recognized consumer brands. Management expects the purchases of seed maker Burpee and European pet company TRIXIE to unlock new retail relationships and international markets.

The company expanded non-GAAP gross margin to 33.6% in fiscal 2026 by exiting low-margin pet distribution and unprofitable live plant lines. These actions create a baseline of profitability that relies on product mix rather than short-term cost cuts.

E-commerce momentum accelerated across both operating segments, led by over 30% growth in point-of-sale garden e-commerce in the fourth quarter. Expanding digital channels gives the business direct access to consumer buying trends while offsetting swings in retail store traffic.

Headwinds in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 will depress near-term results due to seasonal losses from Burpee, elevated retailer inventory levels, and higher fuel costs. Management is maintaining cost discipline while protecting strategic investments in artificial intelligence and product innovation.

The company maintains a capital posture backed by $1.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents to fund future expansion without issuing new debt. Operational efficiency and expanded retail distribution position the business to compound value as market conditions normalize.
